challenges.instruction: Djoser's stairway to the sky begins on the riverbank. Haul the limestone blocks up to their marks at Saqqara — on wet sand each one slides until something stops it.
challenges.fact: Imhotep designed the Step Pyramid of Djoser around 2650 BCE — the world's first large stone structure. He was later deified as a god of medicine.

challenges.instruction: The builders carved their names and their world into the stone. Fill in the crossword of the words they lived by — pharaoh, pyramid, desert.
challenges.fact: PHARAOH, PYRAMID, DUNE — the vocabulary of a civilisation that Imhotep helped build, raising stone mountains from the desert floor.

challenges.instruction: Six steps, each a mastaba laid on the one below, cased in white Tura limestone. Raise Djoser's pyramid course by course, capstone last.
challenges.fact: The Step Pyramid of Djoser has six tiers and a subterranean maze of corridors. Imhotep designed every one.

challenges.instruction: The apprentice's sum is the one Khufu's builders will face a century after Imhotep. Set the Great Pyramid's height so that it holds all its stone.
challenges.fact: The pyramids were built with a workforce of skilled, paid laborers — not slaves — who received food, medical care, and honored burial near the site.

challenges.instruction: Descend the three levels of corridors beneath the Step Pyramid and reach Djoser's burial chamber at the bottom of the great shaft.
challenges.fact: Beneath the Step Pyramid runs a labyrinth of nearly 6 km of shafts, corridors and galleries. Djoser's granite burial vault lies at the foot of a shaft 28 m deep, and some of the chambers around it were lined with blue faience tiles.

challenges.instruction: The cup-bearer has seized the throne, and the cities of Sumer must learn it. Win the raid: send the target number of your rival's pieces back to the start.
challenges.fact: The Akkadian Empire (c. 2334–2154 BCE) unified diverse Sumerian city-states under a single ruler for the first time in recorded history — a template copied by every empire since.

challenges.instruction: The legend says Aqqi the water-drawer lifted the baby from the river and raised him as his gardener. Work the sluices and water every field, as the young Sargon once did.
challenges.fact: The Legend of Sargon, written down long after his time, has the king tell how his mother set him on the Euphrates in a basket of rushes sealed with bitumen, and how Aqqi the water-drawer lifted him out and raised him as a gardener.

challenges.instruction: Sargon has conquered the city-states. Tour Sumer and win the cities over before Lugalzagesi's loyalists turn them back.
challenges.fact: Sargon of Akkad (c. 2334–2279 BCE) built the world's first empire by combining military conquest with cultural assimilation. His daughter Enheduanna, High Priestess of Ur, is history's first named author.

challenges.instruction: Sargon's empire lived on its trade as well as its armies. Sail his route from the quay of Akkad to Meluhha and come home with a fortune.
challenges.fact: Sargon of Akkad (c. 2334–2279 BCE) created history's first empire, uniting dozens of city-states under one ruler for the first time. His daughter Enheduanna became history's first named author.

story: The King and the Wild Man

challenges.instruction: Enkidu runs with the gazelles and fills in the trapper's pits. Ring the herd at the watering hole so that none strays toward the snares.
challenges.fact: The Epic of Gilgamesh, preserved on twelve clay tablets, predates Homer's Iliad by at least 1,500 years. It contains a great flood story remarkably similar to Noah's in the Bible.

challenges.instruction: Gilgamesh boasts of the walls he built and the battles he won. Aga of Kish has come against Uruk — hold the walls.
challenges.fact: The Sumerian King List names Gilgamesh as the fifth king of the First Dynasty of Uruk; if he lived, he reigned around 2700 BCE. The kings of Ur, six centuries later, still called him their brother.

challenges.instruction: In the shepherds' camp Shamhat teaches Enkidu the ways of men — bread, beer and the games of the city. Beat her at twenty squares.
challenges.fact: Enkidu's journey from wilderness to brotherhood mirrors humanity's own emergence — his taming by a priestess represents the Mesopotamian belief that civilisation elevated human beings above the animals they had once lived among.

challenges.instruction: Brothers now, Gilgamesh and Enkidu go out in search of glory. Fight through the lion of the pass, Humbaba of the Cedar Forest and the Bull of Heaven.
challenges.fact: Enkidu and Gilgamesh fought briefly at the city gate, but quickly became the closest of friends. Enkidu's death from divine punishment drives the epic's second half and Gilgamesh's desperate quest for immortality.

challenges.instruction: Enkidu is dead, and Gilgamesh will not accept it. Cross the frozen passes to the mountain of the sun, on the road to the one man who escaped death.
challenges.fact: Gilgamesh's search leads to Utnapishtim, survivor of the Flood, whom the gods made immortal. His account of the deluge in Tablet XI is so close to the story of Noah that George Smith's reading of it in London in 1872 caused a sensation.

challenges.instruction: The quest ends beside a pool. Put the story of the plant of youth back in order, from the bottom of the sea to the serpent.
challenges.fact: Even in failure the epic gives its answer: the plant is lost, but Gilgamesh comes home and shows Urshanabi the walls of Uruk — the work of his that will last.

challenges.instruction: Gilgamesh sees the walls of Uruk with new eyes. Lay the brickwork true and keep the gates open — this is what will outlast him.
challenges.fact: The epic ends where it began, on the wall of Uruk: “Go up on the wall and walk around… a square mile is city, a square mile date-grove, a square mile clay-pit, half a square mile the temple of Ishtar.”

challenges.instruction: Fight lesson 1 · First Duel. Deploy Gilgamesh to Uruk, add the Warrior, then tap Gilgamesh and tap Ashurbanipal to attack. Win one attack.
challenges.fact: In a Local Event every card at the location counts: Gilgamesh brings 10 Strength, the Warrior adds +2 (or +4 beside a Great Person who shares that identity), and the higher total wins the attack. The loser returns to its owner's hand unless Kill mode is on.

challenges.instruction: The king's agents ride for Babylon, Nippur and Uruk with a list in hand. Bring back only the tablets Ashurbanipal has asked for.
challenges.fact: Cuneiform tablets were written in vertical columns read top to bottom, right to left. Ashurbanipal's library catalogue tablets — listing every text by first line — are among the oldest library indexes ever found. The Epic of Gilgamesh was filed under its opening words: 'He who saw the deep.'

challenges.instruction: The carts of tablets keep coming and the palace guards have time on their hands. Play the guards' game in the courtyard while the scribes unload.
challenges.fact: The burning of Nineveh paradoxically preserved Ashurbanipal's library. The fire baked the clay tablets hard, protecting them. The library lay buried until Austen Henry Layard rediscovered it in 1849, bringing the Epic of Gilgamesh back to the world.

challenges.instruction: Organise them by subject, says the king. Shelve each work with the subject it belongs to.
challenges.fact: Ashurbanipal could read and write in multiple languages — an extraordinary feat for a king. He boasted of this in inscriptions, proud of mastering both the scribal arts and the military campaigns typical of Assyrian rulers.

challenges.instruction: Nineveh burns: the fire bakes the clay and cracks the stone. Fit the shattered pieces of the palace reliefs back into their outlines.
challenges.fact: Ashurbanipal sent scribes across his empire to copy every text they could find — myths, astronomy, medicine, and administration. Catalogue tablets listing the library's contents show it was deliberately organised by subject — the world's first planned library. The Epic of Gilgamesh was found among its holdings.

challenges.instruction: Copy it carefully. Check each sign of the Gilgamesh tablet against the scribes' sign list and read out its famous first line.
challenges.fact: Nineveh fell in 612 BCE to a coalition of Babylonians, Medes, and Scythians. The city was so thoroughly sacked that the Greek historian Xenophon marched past its ruins 200 years later without knowing what it had been. The library survived only because fire baked the clay tablets into permanence.

challenges.instruction: Ashurbanipal's library lay buried for 2,500 years under the mound of Kuyunjik. Dig where the shards point and recover the tablet caches before the season ends.
challenges.fact: When Nineveh fell in 612 BCE the palace burned — and the fire baked Ashurbanipal's clay tablets hard, preserving them. Excavated in the 1850s, they gave the world back the Epic of Gilgamesh, the Babylonian flood story and much of what is known of Mesopotamian medicine, omens and law.

challenges.instruction: Fight lesson 1 · First Duel. Deploy Ashurbanipal to Uruk, add the Sovereign, then tap Ashurbanipal and tap Nakht to attack. Win one attack.
challenges.fact: In a Local Event every card at the location counts: Ashurbanipal brings 8 Politics, the Sovereign adds +2 (or +4 beside a Great Person who shares that identity), and the higher total wins the attack. The loser returns to its owner's hand unless Kill mode is on.

challenges.instruction: The thread keeps unwinding from the cocoon in Lei Zu's cup. How long is it? Add each length to the count as it comes off.
challenges.fact: Chinese tradition credits Lei Zu (also written Leizu or Si Ling-chi), wife of the Yellow Emperor Huangdi, with discovering silk around 2700 BCE when a silkworm cocoon fell into her tea and she unravelled its thread.

challenges.instruction: Silkworms eat nothing but mulberry leaves. Lead water to the mulberry grove so that the palace worms never go hungry.
challenges.fact: Chinese tradition credits Lei Zu with teaching people to plant mulberries and raise silkworms as well as to reel silk. Sericulture became women's work, and empresses performed a yearly rite of gathering mulberry leaves.

challenges.instruction: Guard the secret carefully. Raise a rammed-earth wall around the silk-house, one tamped layer at a time.
challenges.fact: China kept sericulture to itself for thousands of years. By one legend the secret left only when a Chinese princess, married to the king of Khotan, smuggled silkworm eggs out in her headdress — a story recorded by the pilgrim Xuanzang in the 7th century.

challenges.instruction: Lei Zu's thread will one day cross the world. Lead a caravan from Chang'an to Constantinople and sell the silk where it is rarest.
challenges.fact: Silk reached Rome through many middlemen. In 14 CE the Senate forbade men to wear it, and Pliny the Elder complained that India, China and Arabia drained a hundred million sesterces a year from the empire for luxuries.

challenges.instruction: Lei Zu learned by noticing small patterns. Restore the dots on the Luo River turtle's shell so that every line has the same sum.
challenges.fact: The Lo Shu is among the oldest magic squares known. Chinese tradition ties it to Yu the Great, the legendary tamer of floods, who is placed a few centuries after the Yellow Emperor and Lei Zu.

challenges.instruction: The greatest discoveries wait for someone patient enough to notice. Study the shape while it is shown, then build it from memory.
challenges.fact: Lei Zu's story comes from later texts, but archaeology bears out the age of Chinese silk: woven silk from about 2700 BCE has been found in Zhejiang, and traces of silk protein in tombs at Jiahu are some 8,500 years old.

challenges.instruction: Fight lesson 1 · First Duel. Deploy Lei Zu to Memphis, add the Noble, then tap Lei Zu and tap Ashurbanipal to attack. Win one attack.
challenges.fact: In a Local Event every card at the location counts: Lei Zu brings 10 Wealth, the Noble adds +2 (or +4 beside a Great Person who shares that identity), and the higher total wins the attack. The loser returns to its owner's hand unless Kill mode is on.

challenges.instruction: To Hesy-Ra the body is a system of channels running out from the heart. Turn the vessels until the heart reaches every part — then the whole body can be read.
challenges.fact: Hesy-Ra (c. 2700–2600 BCE) is the earliest known physician in recorded history. He held the title 'Chief of Dentists and Physicians' — inscribed on a wooden panel in his tomb at Saqqara, making him the first named doctor in history.

challenges.instruction: The Pharaoh has not slept for three nights. Gather from the physician's stores everything the remedy for his tooth will need.
challenges.fact: Hesy-Ra was Chief of Dentists and Physicians under Pharaoh Djoser (c. 2650 BCE). The Step Pyramid at Saqqara, designed by Imhotep, was built during the same reign — making Hesy-Ra and Imhotep contemporaries at the world's most ambitious construction project.

challenges.instruction: Juniper, honey and ground malachite: pack the cavity firmly, layer by layer, and leave no gap for the rot to return.
challenges.fact: Ancient Egyptian medical knowledge was remarkably advanced. The Edwin Smith Papyrus describes 48 surgical cases with diagnoses, treatments, and prognoses — a clinical approach that would not be surpassed in Europe for thousands of years.

challenges.instruction: Hesy-Ra's tomb is painted with everything he will need in eternity, a senet board among it. Play the game of Djoser's court against one of its scribes.
challenges.fact: Hesy-Ra's tomb at Saqqara is famous for its carved wooden panels, which show him with a scribe's palette and a staff of office, and for a painted corridor picturing his grave goods — chests, vessels, tools and game boards.

challenges.instruction: The carvers have cut Hesy-Ra's titles as a mirror image, to face him from the far side of the panel. Read what they say.
challenges.fact: Egyptian medicine was practised in temple 'Houses of Life' — scriptorium-hospitals where physicians copied medical papyri alongside religious texts. Hesy-Ra's work as both scribe and physician reflects this union of healing and sacred knowledge.

challenges.instruction: Fight lesson 1 · First Duel. Deploy Hesy-Ra to Memphis, add the Doctor, then tap Hesy-Ra and tap Lei Zu to attack. Win one attack.
challenges.fact: In a Local Event every card at the location counts: Hesy-Ra brings 9 Technique, the Doctor adds +2 (or +4 beside a Great Person who shares that identity), and the higher total wins the attack. The loser returns to its owner's hand unless Kill mode is on.

challenges.instruction: Who inherits, and in what order: write it so that no prince can jump the line. Move the royal line one step at a time, never a greater above a lesser.
challenges.fact: The Hittite royal family had suffered generations of murder, coup and revenge over the throne. Telepinu's Edict (c. 1500 BCE) fixed the order of succession and forbade the killing of royal kin — replacing blood with law.

challenges.instruction: The princes will not like the price of breaking this law. Weigh out the silver that the law demands, shekel by shekel, until the penalty is paid.
challenges.fact: The Hittite Empire (c. 1700–1200 BCE) was based in Hattusa, near modern Boğazkale in Turkey. At its peak it rivalled Egypt — and the Hittite-Egyptian clash at Kadesh (c. 1274 BCE) is the first well-documented pitched battle in recorded history.

challenges.instruction: A kingdom strong enough that its succession is boring: raise the gates of Hattusa stone on stone, each passage closed by its top stone.
challenges.fact: Telepinu's Edict predates Greek democratic codes by centuries. Its core principle — that even kings must follow established succession rules — represented a revolutionary idea: that the most powerful rulers were subject to written law.

challenges.instruction: Telepinu needs the panku, the assembly of Hittite nobles, to back his succession law. Work the nobles one by one before the vote is called.
challenges.fact: The Hittite pankus — an assembly of nobles — had real power to check the king. Telepinu's Edict was partly designed to give this body constitutional authority, so that future kings could not simply murder their way to the throne. It was one of history's first constitutional checks on royal power.

challenges.instruction: Let this tablet outlast every king whose name is on it. Fit the cut blocks into the monument's outline — one stray block does not belong.
challenges.fact: Hattusa was abandoned around 1200 BCE and its archives lay buried until 1906, when excavations at Boğazköy began to recover some 30,000 clay tablets and fragments — the Edict of Telepinu among them.

challenges.fact: In a Local Event every card at the location counts: King Telepinu brings 9 Belief, the Monastic adds +2 (or +4 beside a Great Person who shares that identity), and the higher total wins the attack. The loser returns to its owner's hand unless Kill mode is on.

challenges.instruction: Prince Vardhamana leaves his palace on the night the moon stands in Hastottara. Find the moon's lodgings among the stars.
challenges.fact: Mahavira added the fifth vow — Brahmacharya — to the four already taught by the previous Tirthankara. Together, these five vows form the ethical core of Jain monasticism, practised by Jain monks today with the same rigour as in Mahavira's time, over 2,500 years ago.

challenges.instruction: How can a person live without causing harm? Begin with the path under your feet: find every small creature on the road before you take a step.
challenges.fact: Mahavira's first vow, ahimsa, forbids harming any living being, down to insects and the smallest creatures. Jain monks strain their drinking water, and many wear a cloth over the mouth, for the same reason.

challenges.instruction: Ahimsa is a direction, not a rule: act with the least harm you can. Build each figure with as few turns as possible — no needless movement.
challenges.fact: Ahimsa (non-violence) is the supreme ethical principle of Jainism, elevated by Mahavira. It extends to all living beings — including insects. Jain monks carry brooms to sweep the path before them so they do not accidentally step on any creature.

challenges.instruction: Mahavira's teaching would shape India for 2,500 years, down to the yantra carved at a Jain temple in Khajuraho. Complete its square, where even the broken diagonals agree.
challenges.fact: Ahimsa passed from the Jains into Indian life for 2,500 years. Gandhi, who grew up in Gujarat among Jains, named the Jain teacher Shrimad Rajchandra as one of the three people who most shaped his thinking.

challenges.instruction: There is no enemy outside: anger, pride, deceit and greed are the enemies. Slide them aside and let the soul rise to the top.
challenges.fact: Jina means “conqueror” — one who has conquered the inner passions — and Jainism takes its name from it. Mahavira, “Great Hero”, is a title; his birth name was Vardhamana.

challenges.instruction: A disciple has written the teacher's words in a folded alphabet. Read what governs the universe.
challenges.fact: Jainism is unique among major world religions in completely rejecting the concept of a creator god. The universe, in Jain philosophy, is eternal and uncreated. Karma operates as an impersonal natural law — not divine judgment — and liberated souls reach a state of perfect knowledge but do not intervene in worldly affairs.

challenges.instruction: Fight lesson 1 · First Duel. Deploy Mahavira to Memphis, add the Prophet, then tap Mahavira and tap King Telepinu to attack. Win one attack.
challenges.fact: In a Local Event every card at the location counts: Mahavira brings 12 Belief, the Prophet adds +2 (or +4 beside a Great Person who shares that identity), and the higher total wins the attack. The loser returns to its owner's hand unless Kill mode is on.

challenges.instruction: Nakht knows from Sirius when the flood will come. Open the dykes in time so that every basin drinks and the village stays dry.
challenges.fact: Egypt's year had three seasons named for the river: Akhet, the inundation; Peret, the growing; and Shemu, the harvest. An astronomer of Amun like Nakht watched the sky to say when each would begin.

challenges.instruction: Nakht wants the harvesters' faces painted as they really are. Mix the red-brown the painters use for men's skin until it matches the wall.
challenges.fact: The tomb of Nakht (TT52) is a single small painted chapel, yet its scenes of harvest, of fowling in the marshes and of a banquet with a blind harpist and women musicians are among the best-known paintings of ancient Egypt.

challenges.instruction: Nakht counts the harvesters' labour seed by seed. Sow round the fields and bring in more of the grain than the overseer.
challenges.fact: Scribes recorded every harvest for the temple granaries: fields were measured with knotted ropes, the standing crop was assessed for tax, and the grain was counted into the stores measure by measure.

challenges.instruction: In his tomb Nakht's journey goes on. Play senet, the game of passing, against the temple scribe.
challenges.fact: The heliacal rising of Sirius — called Sopdet by Egyptians — occurred just before the Nile's annual flood. This celestial signal was so important that the Egyptian calendar year began on this day. Astronomer-officials like Nakht were responsible for predicting it.

challenges.instruction: The stars are Nakht's clock, calendar and map. Name the star groups of the night as the hour-watchers of Amun did.
challenges.fact: Egyptian priests calculated the solar year at 365 days — off by only a quarter-day. They tracked the sun's annual path using shadow clocks and star tables. The geometry of circles, arcs, and angles was essential astronomical knowledge long before Greek mathematicians formalised it.

challenges.instruction: Fight lesson 1 · First Duel. Deploy Nakht to Memphis, add the Official, then tap Nakht and tap Peseshet to attack. Win one attack.
challenges.fact: In a Local Event every card at the location counts: Nakht brings 7 Politics, the Official adds +2 (or +4 beside a Great Person who shares that identity), and the higher total wins the attack. The loser returns to its owner's hand unless Kill mode is on.

challenges.instruction: Before a single spell is carved, the draughtsmen rule the walls into squares. Lay out the first figure on the grid.
challenges.fact: The tomb of Pediamenopet at Thebes (TT33) holds the largest collection of funerary texts in Egypt, drawn from the Pyramid Texts, the Coffin Texts, the Book of the Dead and the books of the underworld such as the Amduat.

challenges.instruction: Assyrian soldiers idle by the temple gate over a board scratched in the stone. Keep them at their game — and their eyes off the tomb — by beating them at it.
challenges.fact: Pediamenopet lived during the Late Period, a turbulent age of foreign invasions. His vast tomb was a monument so packed with sacred texts that no conqueror's curse could erase all of them. Scholars are still copying and translating them today.

challenges.instruction: These texts guide the soul through death, and the Book of the Dead promises the blessed a game of senet in the hereafter. Win the game of passing.
challenges.fact: The Book of the Dead (more accurately 'Book of Coming Forth by Day') was a personal funerary guide. Spell 125, the Weighing of the Heart, was the most critical: the deceased's heart was weighed against the feather of Ma'at. A heart heavier than the feather — burdened by sins — was devoured by the monster Ammit.

challenges.instruction: Every text in its place and none repeated: lay out the panels of spells on the wall before the carvers begin.
challenges.fact: Pediamenopet held the title Chief Lector Priest — the priest who read the sacred books aloud during the rituals — which may explain why his tomb became a library of sacred texts.

challenges.instruction: What he carves into this limestone will outlast the Assyrians. Build the great gateway of his tomb course by course, the cornice last.
challenges.fact: Pediamenopet's tomb contains texts copied from sources spanning 2,000 years — from Old Kingdom pyramid texts to New Kingdom funerary literature. His scribes were the original archivists, assembling a complete library of the afterlife's instruction manual in one underground room.

challenges.instruction: Fight lesson 1 · First Duel. Deploy Pediamenopet to Memphis, add the Priest, then tap Pediamenopet and tap Peseshet to attack. Win one attack.
challenges.fact: In a Local Event every card at the location counts: Pediamenopet brings 9 Belief, the Priest adds +2 (or +4 beside a Great Person who shares that identity), and the higher total wins the attack. The loser returns to its owner's hand unless Kill mode is on.

challenges.instruction: Peseshet's students learn from old papyri, worn and stained by damp. Restore the picture on the teaching sheet from the clues that survive.
challenges.fact: Peseshet (c. 2500–2450 BCE) is the earliest known female medical administrator in history. Her title 'Imy-r swnwt' — 'Lady Overseer of Female Physicians' — indicates she supervised a group of female medical practitioners, making her a pioneering figure in both medicine and women's leadership.

challenges.instruction: The young physician asks what the law allows. Peseshet points to her own title, cut in mirror letters on the wall — read it.
challenges.fact: Peseshet predates Hippocrates — the 'Father of Medicine' — by nearly 2,000 years. Her title 'Lady Overseer of Female Physicians' implies there were enough women doctors to require an administrator, suggesting female medical practice was established, not exceptional.

challenges.instruction: The patient in front of you needs a remedy now. Measure out the dose, joining the small parts of the hekat until it is exactly right.
challenges.fact: We know of Peseshet entirely through a false door stele in her son's tomb at Giza. This was a common way for high-status women to be memorialized. The inscription preserves for 4,500 years the name of the world's first known female physician.

challenges.instruction: Peseshet's school teaches the scribes' arithmetic along with medicine. Take the lesson beside the new pyramids of Giza and measure one by its shadow.
challenges.fact: The Great Pyramid of Giza, raised within a century of Peseshet's career, is set square to the four cardinal points to within a fraction of a degree, and its 230-metre base is level to about two centimetres.

challenges.instruction: Peseshet's name will be kept in her son's tomb at Giza, among the things the dead take with them. Play senet with a student in the physicians' hall.
challenges.fact: A false door was the place in an Egyptian tomb where the living set down offerings and the spirit of the dead was believed to pass between worlds. Peseshet's own false door was set up in the tomb of her son Akhethotep.

challenges.fact: In a Local Event every card at the location counts: Peseshet brings 8 Intelligence, the Astronomer adds +2 (or +4 beside a Great Person who shares that identity), and the higher total wins the attack. The loser returns to its owner's hand unless Kill mode is on.

challenges.question: Euclid worked in which great ancient city?
challenges.fact: Euclid worked at the Library of Alexandria under Ptolemy I around 300 BCE. When Ptolemy asked if there was a shorter way to learn geometry, Euclid reportedly replied: 'There is no royal road to geometry.'

challenges.instruction: Ptolemy wants a shortcut, a student wants a profit, a sceptic wants a picture. Answer each of them as Euclid did — with proof.
challenges.fact: Euclid's Elements (c. 300 BCE) comprises 13 books and 465 propositions. It was used in university geometry courses until the early 20th century — over 2,000 years of continuous use.

challenges.instruction: The Elements begins with definitions and builds every proof on them. Fill the crossword with the words Euclid's geometry starts from.
challenges.fact: Euclid's proof of the Pythagorean theorem occupies a full page of the Elements and uses nothing but logic. It remains one of the most beautiful proofs in all of mathematics.

challenges.instruction: Eratosthenes, librarian at Alexandria, turned Euclid's geometry on the Earth itself. Read the gnomon's noon shadow and measure the planet.
challenges.fact: Eratosthenes' method rests on a theorem of the Elements: a straight line falling on two parallel lines makes the alternate angles equal (Book I, Proposition 29). The sun's rays at Syene and Alexandria are the parallels.

params.title: The Scrolls of the Mouseion
params.intro: New scrolls have come to Alexandria and the catalogue slips are mixed. Match each Greek author with the work the scholars of the Mouseion copied and studied.
params.fact: Under Ptolemy I and II the Mouseion of Alexandria gathered scholars and books from the whole Greek world. Callimachus later catalogued the Library in his Pinakes, 120 books of lists of authors and their works.

challenges.instruction: The scholars who came after Euclid built on the Library's books. Match each author to the scroll Alexandria kept — before the slips shift again.
challenges.fact: Euclid's Elements was copied and commented on at Alexandria for centuries. Theon of Alexandria's edition of the 4th century CE is the source of almost every manuscript that survives.

challenges.instruction: Fight lesson 2 · Strength in Numbers. Over two turns stack Euclid, Chanakya and both followers at Carthage, then win two attacks against the rival side.
challenges.fact: An attack compares whole sides at a location, not single cards. Two Great People and two followers in the same stat outweigh a rival who arrived first, and each win sends one rival card back to its owner's hand.

challenges.instruction: Not every Athenian wants the allies' tribute spent on temples. Thucydides son of Melesias is stirring up the countryside — tour the demes of Attica and win them for Pericles' building programme.
challenges.fact: The quarrel over the building programme was settled by ostracism around 443 BCE: Thucydides son of Melesias was sent into exile for ten years, and Pericles was elected general year after year until his death.

params.title: The Owls of Athens
params.intro: Strike Laurion silver from tiny obols up to the four-drachma owl — and on to the talents of the treasury.
params.fact: Athens struck its silver tetradrachms, stamped with Athena and her owl, from the mines of Laurion. In 454 BCE the treasury of the Delian League was moved from Delos to Athens, and Pericles spent its tribute on the Acropolis.
params.twistText: Laurion silver: a raw lump of silver merges with any coin and lifts it one tier — but two lumps will not merge. Save them for the coin that needs them.

challenges.instruction: Aspasia's salon talks philosophy, but the city outside runs on silver. Strike Laurion silver up to the owl that carries Athens' name across the Aegean.
challenges.fact: Athenian owls were trusted so widely that they were imitated from Egypt to Arabia. 'Owls to Athens' was a Greek saying for something pointless — Aristophanes uses it in The Birds.

challenges.instruction: Pleistoanax's warning becomes an army: in 446 BCE the Peloponnesians march into Attica. Post the Athenian archers along the road from Eleusis so the invaders cannot reach the city.
challenges.fact: Pericles dominated Athenian politics for three decades through strategic alliances and oratorical power — power that his enemies claimed was shaped by Aspasia.

challenges.instruction: Pericles must win a majority in the Athenian Assembly to fund the Parthenon from Delian League tribute. Lobby the tribes before Thucydides son of Melesias turns them.
challenges.fact: The Parthenon (447–432 BCE) was built under Pericles' direction. It took fifteen years, 20,000 workers and 13,400 blocks of Pentelic marble cut to tolerances of 0.2 mm.

challenges.instruction: Aspasia is on trial in Athens. Defend her reputation with the right arguments before the jury.
challenges.fact: Pericles wept openly before the jury defending Aspasia — an extraordinary breach of Athenian decorum. She was acquitted. His tears won more votes than the logic.

challenges.instruction: While Aspasia's enemies attack in court, the work on the Acropolis goes on. Every column rises from numbered marble drums: push each drum onto its own base.
challenges.fact: Each Doric column of the Parthenon was built up from about ten to twelve drums of Pentelic marble, quarried on Mount Pentelikon some 16 km from the Acropolis and fluted only after the column stood. Pheidias oversaw the works for Pericles.

challenges.instruction: War comes at last. Pericles brings the people of Attica inside the Long Walls and lets the Spartans burn the fields — place walls and towers so no raiding party reaches the city.
challenges.fact: In the winter of 431 BCE Pericles gave the Funeral Oration for the war's first dead, as Thucydides records it: 'the whole earth is the tomb of famous men.' In Plato's Menexenus, Socrates teases that Aspasia composed it.

challenges.instruction: What outlasted the war was what Athens built and sang. Raise the Odeon of Pericles course by course, its peaked roof last.
challenges.fact: The Parthenon (447–432 BCE) was built with astonishing precision: its columns taper, its platform curves, and its lines are never quite straight — all deliberate optical corrections to make the building appear perfect to the human eye. Greek architecture and geometry were inseparable.

challenges.instruction: Step into Cicero's sandals: count heads and win over the senators one by one, so the vote to act against Catiline's conspirators carries.
challenges.fact: Cicero's four Catilinarian Orations (63 BCE) are among history's most famous speeches. He secured the Senate's vote to execute the conspirators — and was later exiled for putting Roman citizens to death without trial.

challenges.instruction: Law, Cicero says, is the bond of the state — and a sound argument leaves an opponent nowhere to go. Find the move that corners him.
challenges.fact: Cicero's Catilinarian Orations cornered the conspirators so completely that even Catiline's allies abandoned him. His rhetoric was his weapon.

challenges.instruction: Cicero has spoken out against Antony fourteen times, and now a friend sends word in Caesar's old cipher. Turn the wheel to learn whose hand is raised against him.
challenges.fact: After Caesar's assassination, Cicero attacked Mark Antony in the speeches called the Philippics. Antony had him killed in 43 BCE, and his head and hands — which had spoken and written them — were nailed up on the Rostra in the Forum.

challenges.instruction: Cicero loved the wonders of Greek learning, none more than Archimedes' sphere, carried to Rome from Syracuse. Restore its lost wheels so the moon keeps time again.
challenges.fact: More of Cicero's writing survives than of any other Roman: speeches, books of philosophy and rhetoric, and more than 900 letters, many to his friend Atticus. They make him the best-documented person of the ancient world.

challenges.instruction: A republic shows its worth in public works, Cicero wrote — walls, harbours, aqueducts. Route the Aqua Marcia from the Anio springs into Rome.
challenges.fact: The Aqua Marcia entered Rome on arches and carried water up to the Capitol. Two later aqueducts, the Tepula and the Julia, were built on top of its arcades, three channels sharing one line of arches.

challenges.instruction: Anaxagoras turns his students' eyes to the night sky over Athens: these are not gods but stones on fire. Find each figure he names among the stars.
challenges.fact: Around 450 BCE, Anaxagoras was charged with impiety for saying the sun was a fiery rock larger than the Peloponnese. He was saved from execution by his friend Pericles but exiled from Athens.

challenges.instruction: Zeno trusts reason over the senses; Anaxagoras reasons from what he sees. Set the sun so the 2 m post throws a 10 m shadow, and read the sun's height from the shadow alone.
challenges.fact: Anaxagoras correctly deduced that the moon shines with reflected sunlight, that eclipses occur when the moon covers the sun, and that the sun is a glowing rock. All this 2,500 years before telescopes.

challenges.instruction: Anaxagoras held that Nous (Mind) imposes order on chaos — each element in its proper place. Fill the grid so each row, column, and 2×2 box contains 1–4 exactly once.
challenges.fact: Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE) was the first to introduce Nous — cosmic Mind — as the ordering principle of the universe. He correctly deduced that the moon shines with reflected sunlight and that eclipses are caused by the moon blocking the sun.

challenges.instruction: The questions Zeno and Anaxagoras argue over were first asked in the Ionian cities. Link the schools of philosophy so that every city is joined to the rest.
challenges.fact: The pre-Socratics were the first to explain nature without myth. Their debate between flux (Heraclitus) and permanence (Parmenides) set up every major argument in Western philosophy that followed.

challenges.instruction: Anaxagoras said the moon has no light of its own — it shines with the sun's. Place the mirror so the sun's beam reaches the far corner, as sunlight reaches the moon.
challenges.fact: Anaxagoras was the first to correctly explain lunar phases and eclipses: the moon reflects the sun's light and the earth's shadow causes eclipses. He deduced this by reasoning about light and geometry, 2,500 years before anyone could test it directly.

challenges.instruction: Even the Nile was a question for reason: Anaxagoras said its summer flood was melting snow from Ethiopia. Work the sluices so the flood waters every basin and spares the village.
challenges.fact: Anaxagoras spent his last years at Lampsacus on the Hellespont. Asked what honour he wanted, he asked that the children have a holiday every year in the month he died — and Lampsacus kept the custom long after.

challenges.instruction: Mani taught his vision in pictures as well as words. Piece together the page of his Picture Book that shows the battle of Light and Darkness.
challenges.fact: Mani (216–274 CE) founded Manichaeism, a dualistic religion blending Zoroastrian light-and-darkness cosmology, Christian ethics, and Buddhist concepts of spiritual purification. At its height, Manichaeism spread from the Roman Empire to Tang Dynasty China — one of history's most geographically expansive faiths.

challenges.instruction: From Persia, Mani's letters go out to every congregation on the royal roads. Plan a round that carries them to every town and back to the prophet.
challenges.fact: Mani wrote his scriptures himself, in a script adapted from Syriac, so that his teaching would not be corrupted after his death as he believed the teachings of Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus had been.

challenges.instruction: Kartir has turned the king against him, and Mani lies in chains. Read his last message to the church as his disciples signal it, letter by letter.
challenges.fact: Mani's death in 274 CE echoed the martyrdom narratives of the very religions he synthesized. His followers spread his teachings across the Silk Road for centuries — Manichaean texts were still being copied in China in the 13th century.

challenges.instruction: Mani taught through parables — stories of light trapped in darkness. Complete his parable of the soul's journey from matter back to the realm of pure light.
challenges.fact: Mani believed the material world was a prison of darkness and that human souls were fragments of divine light awaiting liberation. His parables, hymns, and paintings were all instruments of the same message: light will eventually triumph over darkness.

challenges.instruction: A thousand years on, Mani's books lay buried in the sand of the Silk Road. Dig the ruins of Kocho and bring them back to the light.
challenges.fact: Mani composed hymnbooks in multiple languages, including Middle Persian, Parthian, and Syriac. The Coptic Manichaean Psalm-Book, discovered in Egypt in 1930, preserves hundreds of hymns that reveal a sophisticated musical tradition within his church.

challenges.instruction: Mulan has left home at dawn in her father's armour, and by dusk she camps by the Yellow River. Take the crossing at first light and reach the northern bank.
challenges.fact: The Ballad of Mulan, a poem dating to the Northern Wei dynasty (386–534 CE), tells of a daughter who disguises herself as a man to spare her aged, ailing father from conscription. She fights for twelve years, earns high honours, and then reveals her identity — astonishing her comrades.

challenges.instruction: Year after year the Rouran horsemen ride at the Wei border. Post Mulan's archers and catapults along the road so that no raider gets through.
challenges.fact: The ballad's ending is deliberately understated: Mulan's comrades, who fought beside her for a decade, are stunned to discover she is a woman. The poem asks no moral question — it simply presents her choice as natural and her courage as obvious.

params.title: The Ballad of Mulan
params.intro: Home after twelve years. Match each person, place or thing in the ballad with what it brings to her story.
params.twist: Call and answer: the pairs must be found in the order they are called out. A right pair turned up out of turn goes back face down (no mistake, but it costs time).
params.fact: The ballad ends with a riddle: the he-hare kicks his feet, the she-hare narrows her eyes, but when two hares run side by side, who can tell which is he and which is she?
pairs: Meet her at the city wall
Sharpens the knife for a feast

challenges.instruction: Mulan turns down the Khan's honours and rides home. Tell her ballad again from the loom to the two hares: match each person, place and thing to its part in the song, in order.
challenges.fact: Mulan refused the emperor's offer of office and asked only for a fast horse to carry her home. The original ballad ends with her reunited family and Mulan in her women's clothes again — her identity secure, her duty complete, her reward the return of ordinary life.

challenges.instruction: The army marches north through the passes. Lead Mulan's company from the Yellow River by way of the Black Mountain to the Yan Mountains before supplies or days run out.
challenges.fact: The ballad describes a real frontier: the northern Wei territories were under constant pressure from the Rouran Khaganate. The poem's military details — twelve years of campaigns, the yellow river crossing, the Black Mountain pass — reflect genuine geography and the brutal reality of steppe warfare.

challenges.instruction: The last battle is fought on frozen ground. Charge Mulan across the ice — once she is moving she slides until something stops her — and reach the far end.
challenges.fact: The Ballad of Mulan became one of China's most enduring stories because it celebrated filial piety and personal courage simultaneously — two of Confucian culture's highest values. It has been retold in opera, film, and literature across fourteen centuries.

params.title: The War Chest
params.intro: Strike copper kakanis and mashakas up into silver panas and gold suvarnas — enough to pay an army.
params.fact: The Arthashastra puts a master of the mint over the striking of silver and copper coins and an examiner of coins to test them, and fixes fines for anyone who makes or passes false coin. Its rule is blunt: every undertaking depends first on the treasury.
params.twistText: False coin: counterfeits slip into the tray. They never merge with true coins — slide two counterfeits together and the examiner melts them down.

challenges.instruction: Thrown out of the Nanda court with nothing, Chanakya knows a new throne has to be paid for. Strike copper into silver and gold for the war chest — and keep the counterfeits out.
challenges.fact: Chanakya is also called Kautilya or Vishnugupta. He served as advisor to Chandragupta Maurya, the founder of the Maurya Empire, and authored the Arthashastra — an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft and political economy.

challenges.instruction: Chanakya sends Chandragupta his first lesson in the code his spies use, each letter a pair of numbers. Find every letter on the square.
challenges.fact: The Arthashastra (c. 300 BCE) is remarkably pragmatic — Chanakya advises a king to plant spies even in his own court, test ministers with temptations, and treat foreign relations as perpetual competition. Its realpolitik predates Machiavelli's The Prince by nearly 1,800 years.

challenges.instruction: To learn which ministers can be trusted, Chanakya has a letter of treason planted on one of them. Read it in its folded alphabet, as the minister will.
challenges.fact: The Arthashastra devotes entire chapters to managing the king's inner circle — testing ministers with planted temptations, using counterintelligence against spies, and playing factions against each other. Chanakya's political realism was as relevant in the Maurya court as in any modern boardroom.

challenges.instruction: Chandragupta and Chanakya must bind the provinces to the new Maurya throne. Travel the empire and out-canvass the Nanda loyalists.
challenges.fact: The Maurya Empire under Chandragupta extended westward to meet the successor kingdoms of Alexander the Great. Chanakya's Arthashastra describes in detail how to manage the governors of conquered territories — through a combination of incentives, surveillance, and the projection of royal legitimacy.

challenges.instruction: To hold a frontier on the Hindu Kush, Chandragupta's army must face the Macedonians of Seleucus at the Indus. Choose the right weapon for each enemy.
challenges.fact: Under Chandragupta Maurya and his grandson Ashoka, the Maurya Empire became one of the largest empires of the ancient world, spanning from modern Afghanistan across the entire subcontinent to Bengal. At its peak under Ashoka (c. 268–232 BCE), it covered about 5 million square kilometres — the first political unification of India.

challenges.instruction: The Arthashastra counts war elephants as a kingdom's greatest strength. Guide a wild herd into the stockade — post beaters to close every path out of the forest.
challenges.fact: Seleucus I ceded the Maurya Empire's western provinces to Chandragupta around 303 BCE in return for 500 war elephants. Those elephants helped Seleucus win the Battle of Ipsus two years later — the deal Kautilya's statecraft made possible reshaped the Hellenistic world.

params.title: Equal Syllables
params.intro: Valmiki's verse fell into four balanced quarters. Restore the square so every row, column and both long diagonals share one sum.
params.fact: Sanskrit metres are counted in syllables, light and heavy, not in stresses. Pingala's Chandahshastra, a few centuries BCE, set out every pattern of light and heavy syllables — an early cousin of binary counting.

challenges.instruction: The words came out in a rhythm Valmiki had never spoken: four quarters, equal syllables, every part in balance. Make every line of the square balance the same way.
challenges.fact: Tradition calls Valmiki the Adi Kavi, the first poet, and his Ramayana the Adi Kavya, the first poem of Sanskrit literature. The epic opens with the story of how he came to poetry, before it tells a single deed of Rama.

challenges.instruction: Brahma has given Valmiki the story of Rama, and it begins with exile. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana have left Ayodhya; take Guha's boat across the Ganga.
challenges.fact: The Ramayana centers on Prince Rama of Ayodhya — his exile with his wife Sita and brother Lakshmana, Sita's abduction by the demon king Ravana, and Rama's journey to rescue her with the help of Hanuman and an army of monkeys. It remains one of Asia's most beloved epics.

challenges.instruction: Valmiki's verses follow Rama south. Lead the exiles from Chitrakuta to Panchavati, where Sita is taken, then to Kishkindha and the shore of the southern sea.
challenges.fact: The Ramayana's themes — the duty of a prince, the devotion of a wife, the loyalty of a friend — have resonated across Asia for 2,500 years. The epic has more than 300 known versions across South and Southeast Asia, each reflecting the values of its culture.

challenges.instruction: Every telling of the Ramayana goes back to one riverbank. Put the moment in order — the river, the two birds, the hunter's arrow and the verse that grief made.
challenges.fact: The shloka metre — the pattern Valmiki invented in that moment of grief — became the dominant verse form of Sanskrit epic poetry. The Mahabharata, the Puranas, and thousands of religious texts all use the same metre that Valmiki created spontaneously, in sorrow, beside a river.

challenges.instruction: The war that ends the tale: Rama faces Ravana's champions at Lanka. Choose the right weapon for each foe — the poem that tells it will outlast every king.
challenges.fact: The Ramayana has influenced cultures across Southeast Asia for over a thousand years. Thailand has the Ramakien, Indonesia has the Kakawin Ramayana, and Cambodia's Reamker is performed at the royal court. Puppetry and dance forms based on the Ramayana are UNESCO-listed cultural traditions in Malaysia, Thailand, and Myanmar.

challenges.instruction: Condemned and exiled, Pleistoanax flees to Mount Lycaeum in the dead of winter. Slide down the frozen slopes to the precinct of Zeus, where Sparta cannot touch him.
challenges.fact: Pleistoanax was exiled in 445 BCE after being accused of accepting bribes from Pericles to withdraw the Spartan army from Attica. He spent nineteen years in exile near Mount Lycaeum before being recalled.

challenges.instruction: Without their king, the Spartans march into Attica year after year and come home with nothing. Show the elders what a king could do: outmanoeuvre the Athenian forces.
challenges.fact: Thucydides reports that Pleistoanax's enemies accused him of bribing the priestess at Delphi, who told every Spartan embassy to bring back the seed of the demigod son of Zeus from a foreign land, or plough with a silver ploughshare.

challenges.instruction: At last the ephors send for him. A leather strip arrives on Mount Lycaeum — find the rod that makes it read.
challenges.fact: When Sparta recalled Pleistoanax, around 427 BCE, Thucydides says it welcomed him home with the same dances and sacrifices as when its first kings were installed at the founding of Lacedaemon.

challenges.instruction: Back on the throne, Pleistoanax leads the Spartans out once more — into Parrhasia, to free the Arcadians from Mantinea. Choose the right weapon for each defender.
challenges.fact: The Peace of Nicias (421 BCE) was negotiated largely by Pleistoanax on the Spartan side. It was meant to last fifty years, but it lasted less than seven before the Sicilian Expedition shattered it.

challenges.instruction: Parmenides' critics call his One absurd. Zeno answers by showing their own view is worse — pick the argument that turns each objection back on itself.
challenges.fact: Achilles and the Tortoise argues that before catching the tortoise, Achilles must reach its starting point — by which time it has moved. This repeats infinitely, seemingly making overtaking impossible. Calculus resolved it 2,000 years later.

challenges.instruction: Half the distance, then half of the rest, then half again. Feel the regress: to move the stack you must first move a smaller one, and before that a smaller one still.
challenges.fact: Zeno's paradoxes were a rhetorical defense of his teacher Parmenides, not his personal beliefs. He used them as reductio ad absurdum — if you accept common sense, you get contradictions. It was a philosophical weapon, not a physics claim.

params.title: Hemmed In
params.intro: Argue as Zeno did: never attack head-on, but close every line your opponent might escape by. Two squares, six pieces each; mills form along the sides, nobody flies, and a side with no move left loses.
params.fact: In Plato's Republic, Adeimantus complains that arguing with a master of question and answer is like playing a board game against a skilled player: step by step the weaker side is hemmed in until it has no move left. Aristotle called Zeno the inventor of dialectic.

challenges.instruction: Zeno never argued head-on: he closed every way out until his opponent had no move left. Play him on the board the same way.
challenges.fact: Zeno's paradoxes were not resolved until Newton and Leibniz developed calculus in the 17th century. The infinite series 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... converges to 1 — Achilles catches the tortoise, and the math finally proved it.

challenges.instruction: In the Stadium paradox, rows of bodies slide past one another and Zeno asks how short a moment can be. Slide the rows back into order.
challenges.fact: The mathematical resolution to Zeno's paradoxes came with calculus: an infinite sum of terms can converge to a finite value. The series ½ + ¼ + ⅛ + … = 1. Newton and Leibniz solved in the 1660s what Zeno posed in 450 BCE — it took 2,100 years to find the right mathematical language.

challenges.instruction: Carthage is yours, but the Vandals let its walls crumble. Rebuild the breached circuit up to the line before Gelimer can return — and keep the gateways open for your army.
challenges.fact: Belisarius retook North Africa from the Vandals in 533–534 and most of Italy from the Ostrogoths in 535–540, briefly restoring much of the old Western Roman Empire to Constantinople. He did it with armies far smaller than his opponents'.

challenges.instruction: The enemy outnumbers you, as it always does. Command Belisarius's amber forces and win with speed and discipline.
challenges.fact: Belisarius won battles against overwhelming odds through disciplined positioning, feigned retreats, and flanking strikes — tactics centuries ahead of his time.

challenges.instruction: Gelimer, the beaten Vandal king, has fled into the mountains. Close every pass so he must surrender — a victory your jealous officers will soon twist into a charge of treason.
challenges.fact: After the conquest of Africa, some of Belisarius's officers wrote secretly to Justinian that he meant to make himself king there. Justinian offered him the choice of staying or coming home; Belisarius sailed at once for Constantinople with Gelimer as his prisoner, and was granted a triumph in 534.

challenges.instruction: Naples will not open its gates. Route your picked men through the old aqueduct channel, under the walls and up into the sleeping city.
challenges.fact: Belisarius besieged Naples in 536 on his way to Rome. After about three weeks, his men discovered that the city's aqueduct, which he had cut, ran beneath the walls; some 400 soldiers crept through it at night and the city fell.

challenges.instruction: At Dara the Persians outnumber you two to one. Place your archers behind the trench before the attack comes, then watch the line hold.
challenges.fact: Belisarius reconquered North Africa and Italy for Justinian with small field armies — about 15,000 men sailed for Africa in 533 — against larger enemies. He relied on disciplined cavalry and mounted archers who could shoot from the saddle, as Procopius stresses.

params.title: Reckoning with Sifr
params.intro: Each rod is a place — ones, tens, hundreds — and an empty rod stands for nothing: the Indians’ zero. Add each amount the market clerk calls out and press Enter; the beads must show the running total.
params.fact: Al-Khwarizmi’s book on Indian reckoning taught place value with nine digits and a zero, which Arabic called sifr, “empty”. Its Latin translation begins “Dixit Algorizmi”, and sifr gave European languages both “cipher” and “zero”.

challenges.instruction: Zero makes the system complete. Reckon the merchant’s sums place by place, and let an empty rod stand for nothing.
challenges.fact: Al-Khwarizmi's 'Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wal-muqabala' (c. 820 CE) — 'The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing' — gave us the word algebra from al-jabr.

challenges.instruction: A coded message has arrived from the House of Wisdom. Decode it letter by letter.
challenges.fact: Al-Khwarizmi's mathematical texts were written in a kind of symbolic code that unlocked the logic of the universe — algebra as a language of hidden structure.

challenges.instruction: Any problem can be reduced and solved step by step. In these same years Alcuin of York set this river puzzle at Charlemagne’s court: find the sequence of crossings that works.
challenges.fact: Al-Khwārizmī's Kitāb al-jabr (c. 820 CE) gave us the word 'algebra.' He illustrated algebraic equations with geometric diagrams, proving solutions by drawing and rearranging squares — the origin of 'completing the square.'

challenges.instruction: In Latin he became Algoritmi, just as Jabir the alchemist became Geber. Follow the steps on Jabir’s scroll to make the target substance: a method, like an algorithm.
challenges.fact: Jabir ibn Hayyan’s writings reached Latin Europe in the 12th century, and later alchemists wrote under his Latinised name, Geber. Al-Khwarizmi’s name went the same way: Algoritmi became “algorithm”.

challenges.instruction: A century later Ibn al-Haytham built on the House of Wisdom’s translations. Make the hole in the wall of the dark room so the candle’s image lands on the marks.
challenges.fact: Ibn al-Haytham, working a century after Al-Khwarizmi, built on the House of Wisdom's translations to write 'Kitab al-Manazir' (Book of Optics) — the first correct account of how vision works. Light enters the eye; the eye does not emit rays.

challenges.instruction: Arrange the opening of One Thousand and One Nights in the correct order — the frame story that gave Scheherazade her voice.
challenges.fact: One Thousand and One Nights was compiled during the Islamic Golden Age (8th–13th centuries) from Persian, Indian, and Arab sources. It reached Europe in Antoine Galland's 1704 French translation, which added stories like Aladdin and Ali Baba that don't appear in the original Arabic manuscripts.

challenges.instruction: Lu Yu burned only charcoal, and gave his brazier three vents to draw the wind. Balance the reactions of the fire: every atom of carbon and oxygen that goes in must come out again.
challenges.fact: Lu Yu's Cha Jing (Classic of Tea, c. 760 CE) has 10 chapters covering tea's origins, tools for processing, making, drinking, and the history of tea. It transformed tea from a medicinal herb into a cultural art form.

challenges.instruction: Brew the tea in the Tang manner Lu Yu set down in the Classic of Tea. Put every step in its proper order.
challenges.fact: Lu Yu insisted on spring water collected before sunrise. He could allegedly identify which mountain spring water came from purely by taste.

challenges.instruction: Lu Yu ranked mountain springs above rivers and wells. Test a spring as water chemists do: titrate its dissolved bicarbonate with dilute acid and stop exactly at the endpoint.
challenges.fact: Lu Yu says to season the water with a little salt at the first boil, to add the powdered tea at the second, and that one sheng of water makes five bowls. Too much water, he warns, and the flavour turns thin.

challenges.instruction: Lu Yu’s rules outlived the Tang: Song tea masters, and later Japan’s tea ceremony, prized iron-glazed tea ware. Give each part of the teapot its oxide, then fire the kiln.
challenges.fact: Tenmoku (天目) glazes — prized in Japanese tea ceremony — used iron oxide to create the signature oil-spot and hare's fur patterns in Song Dynasty kilns.

challenges.fact: Chivalry combined three loyalties: to God (religious duty), to the lord (feudal duty), and to women and the weak (courtly duty). Loyalty to the king was central — a knight who broke this oath was stripped of knighthood.

challenges.instruction: A knight is sworn to protect the weak. Ferry the pilgrims across the river and never leave them outnumbered by bandits on either bank.
challenges.fact: A knight's training took fourteen years. The progression from page to squire to knight was as formalised as any modern profession. The Round Table's innovation — every seat equal, no place more honoured than another — was a radical reimagining of hierarchy in a world of strict rank.

challenges.instruction: Lancelot seeks the Grail, and the monks of the chapel sing the old chant. Arrange the notes of the phrase from low to high.
challenges.fact: The Grail quest is a religious story. In the 13th-century French Quest of the Holy Grail, Lancelot is turned away from the Grail because of his love for Guinevere, and only his son Galahad, the purest knight, achieves it.

params.title: Gwyddbwyll at Camelot
params.intro: A king boxed in by raiders. Unarmed king: he cannot help take a raider, not even as the far side of a sandwich. Your four men must do all the fighting while he runs for a corner.
params.fact: In the Welsh tale The Dream of Rhonabwy, Arthur and Owain play gwyddbwyll on a silver board while their warriors fight. Its rules are lost; some historians think it was a hunt game like the Irish brandubh played here.

challenges.instruction: The true knight serves his king above himself. Lead the king’s few defenders and bring him out to a corner of the board.
challenges.fact: Chivalry evolved over three centuries. Early codes (c.1000 CE) emphasised martial courage; by 1200 CE, troubadour poetry had added courtesy and romantic love. By 1300 CE, protection of the poor and weak entered as the Church sought to direct knightly violence toward Christian purposes.

challenges.instruction: Mix the woad blue worn by medieval knights and dyed across Europe, from Celtic Britain to Charlemagne’s court.
challenges.fact: Woad (Isatis tinctoria) was Europe's primary source of blue dye for millennia. In the 13th century the woad trade was so valuable it funded Gothic cathedrals in France. It was eventually displaced by imported indigo from India, devastating the European woad industry.

challenges.fact: Li Qingzhao (1084–c.1155) is considered the greatest female poet in Chinese history and one of the greatest poets of all. She transformed the ci form — originally sung verses for entertainment — into a vehicle for profound personal expression.

challenges.instruction: Li Qingzhao sets her grief to a tune everyone already knows. Sing her new words to it, note for note, as the melody quickens.
challenges.fact: The ci poems of Li Qingzhao were written to specific tunes — each tune had a name and a set pattern of tones. Her poems about loss, love, and exile have been sung and recited for 900 years.

params.title: Faded Rubbings
params.intro: Damp has got into the last rubbings from the collection: some clues have faded to “?”, and those lines could hold anything. The surviving clues are still enough — work round the gaps.
params.fact: Li Qingzhao and her husband Zhao Mingcheng spent some twenty years gathering rubbings of inscriptions on ancient bronzes and stones. His catalogue of about 2,000 of them, Records on Metal and Stone (Jin Shi Lu), survives with her Postface, written after his death and the loss of most of the originals.

challenges.instruction: Beside the wilting chrysanthemums, Li Qingzhao unrolls a rubbing she once traced with her husband. Restore the faded vessel from the clues that remain.
challenges.fact: Li Qingzhao's life split sharply in two: the happy early years in Jinan collecting and writing beside her husband, and the desolate later years as a refugee. Her poem 'Sheng Sheng Man' opens with eighteen consecutive monosyllables evoking emptiness and longing — one of the most technically daring openings in all of Chinese poetry.

challenges.instruction: What is left of the collection goes south by barge toward the new capital at Hangzhou. Pass the boats through the pound locks without wasting the scarce water.
challenges.fact: Li Qingzhao lost her husband, her home, and her famous art collection when the Jin dynasty invaded northern China in 1127. Her later ci poems are hauntingly different from her earlier joyful verses. She wrote: 'Who is left to share the fragrance of the wine?' — a line that still resonates 900 years later.

params.title: The Emperor Takes to the Sea
params.intro: Winter 1129: Jin cavalry hunt Emperor Gaozong down the coast. Get him to ANY edge square — the open sea — but away from his throne he is weak, taken by just two attackers like any man.
params.fact: When the Jin crossed the Yangtze in 1129, Emperor Gaozong fled to the coast and spent that winter aboard ships off Zhejiang. Li Qingzhao, newly widowed, followed the fleeing court by boat as far as Wenzhou, losing more of the collection at every stop.

challenges.instruction: Li Qingzhao follows the fleeing emperor down the coast with what she can carry. Lead the emperor to the open sea before the Jin riders close the shore.
challenges.fact: In her later ci Li Qingzhao wrote of widowhood and exile in plain, spoken words. In “Spring at Wuling” she says the boats on Twin Streams are too small to carry so much sorrow — a line still quoted for grief that has no place to go.

challenges.instruction: Ryazan is the first city in Batu's path. Close the ring round its walls so the prince cannot break out before the city falls.
challenges.fact: Batu Khan (c.1207–1255) was the grandson of Genghis Khan and founder of the Golden Horde. In 1241, he led the most western Mongol campaign in history, crushing Polish and Hungarian armies simultaneously and reaching the gates of Vienna — before news of Ögedei Khan's death caused the army to withdraw.

params.title: The Ring Round Ryazan, 1237
params.intro: You command the black attackers closing on Ryazan. Keep Prince Yuri from every corner until the moves run out — or surround him for an early win. The edge counts against him.
params.fact: In December 1237 the Mongols ringed Ryazan with a palisade so no one could get in or out, battered the walls with siege engines for five days and stormed the city on 21 December. Prince Yuri Igorevich died with his people; Vladimir fell the following February.

challenges.instruction: Batu's northern wing in Poland and his own army in Hungary must strike within days of each other. Bend the signal through the mirrors so both armies move on the same plan.
challenges.fact: In April 1241 two Mongol forces about 600 km apart won within two days of each other: Baidar and Kadan's wing crushed Duke Henry II of Silesia at Legnica on 9 April, and Batu and Subutai destroyed King Béla IV's Hungarian army at Mohi on 11 April. The Mongols withdrew not because of military defeat but because Ögedei Khan's death required the princes to return east.

challenges.instruction: From his golden tent at Sarai, Batu taxes every caravan that crosses the western steppe. Buy up the caravanserais and outgrow the rival houses before the season ends.
challenges.fact: Batu founded Sarai on the lower Volga as the Golden Horde's capital. It sat on the northern branch of the Silk Road, where caravans carried furs, slaves, silk and silver between the Rus lands, Central Asia and the Black Sea — and the Horde took its tolls on all of it. The Franciscan William of Rubruck, who visited Batu's camp in 1253, described a moving city of tents and wagons.

challenges.instruction: Mongol warriors trained for war through the nerge — a great ring drawn across the steppe. Post your riders to close every gap before the wild horses break out. The same maneuver will encircle armies.
challenges.fact: The nerge was sport and military training at once. Thousands of horsemen spread across the steppe and slowly tightened the ring, and generals studied its coordination problems — timing, signalling over distance, closing both flanks together — then used the same solutions in battle.

challenges.instruction: The European knights cannot resist chasing a fleeing enemy. Let them ride into the trap, then close the ring with one decisive move.
challenges.fact: The feigned retreat was the signature Mongol tactic in Europe. Heavy knights, trained to charge and pursue, could not resist a retreating enemy. The Mongols would fall back for miles, drawing the pursuers into scattered disorder, then wheel and destroy them in detail. European commanders had no answer for an 'enemy' that ran away only to fight on its own terms.

challenges.instruction: The Horde rules from the Volga to Kiev because the khan's word travels fast. Carry his order through every town and back to Sarai, changing horses at the yam stations.
challenges.fact: The Golden Horde that Batu established dominated the Russian steppe for 250 years, collecting tribute from every Russian principality. Moscow grew wealthy as a tax collector for the Horde — a relationship that profoundly shaped Russian political culture, centralizing power and accustoming rulers to absolute authority.

challenges.instruction: The characters are carved and fired hard. Slide the clay type into reading order inside the iron frame, the way Bi Sheng set a page.
challenges.fact: Bi Sheng invented movable type during the Song Dynasty (c.1040 CE) using baked clay — the same material Chinese potters had mastered for thousands of years. Each character was carved in clay, hardened by fire, then set in an iron frame with pine resin. After printing, the resin was heated and the characters removed for reuse.

challenges.instruction: Fire turns soft clay into type that will not soften again. Balance the reactions of Bi Sheng’s kiln and plate: the same atoms must leave as went in.
challenges.fact: Despite its ingenuity, Bi Sheng's clay type did not replace woodblock printing, which remained dominant in China for centuries. Chinese has tens of thousands of characters, making movable type logistically complex — a single print job might require thousands of individual pieces. Woodblock printing remained faster for short texts. Movable type proved more revolutionary in alphabetic languages like Korean and later European languages.

params.title: Counting the Type
params.intro: A page needs many copies of the commonest characters. Add each count the compositor calls out on the counting frame and press Enter — the beads must show the running total.
params.fact: Shen Kuo says Bi Sheng made several pieces of type for every character, and more than twenty for common ones such as 之 and 也, so they could appear many times on one page. A rare character was carved and fired on the spot.

challenges.instruction: Thousands of characters wait in cases labelled by rhyme. Tally how many pieces of the commonest ones the next page will need.
challenges.fact: Bi Sheng's system was described in detail by the statesman Shen Kuo in his 'Dream Pool Essays' (1088 CE) — one of the great scientific documents of the medieval world. Without Shen Kuo's account, we might never have known of Bi Sheng's invention, since none of his actual type survives.

challenges.instruction: Bi Sheng hardened his type in fire, as Song potters hardened their wares. Glaze each band of the vase with the right oxide, then fire the kiln.
challenges.fact: Song Dynasty China (960–1279 CE) was a civilization of extraordinary technological creativity: compass navigation, gunpowder weapons, paper money, paddlewheel ships, and movable type all emerged in a single century. The Song state funded scientific investigation and published encyclopedias — creating the world's first information economy.

challenges.instruction: Shen Kuo, who recorded Bi Sheng’s type, also recorded a spring that turned iron pans to copper. Use the reactivity series to make the salt you are asked for.
challenges.fact: Writing had been recorded on clay tablets since Mesopotamia in 3500 BCE. Bi Sheng's great insight was that clay — the oldest writing substrate in human history — could itself become the tool for mass reproduction of text. He connected the ancient world of clay and the modern world of print in a single creative act.

challenges.instruction: Through Syria and Persia he rides with the caravans, resting at caravanserais a day’s march apart. Buy inns along the road and outtrade the rival merchants before the season ends.
challenges.fact: Ibn Battuta (1304–1368) traveled an estimated 75,000 miles — three times the distance of Marco Polo's journey — visiting the equivalent of 44 modern countries. He crossed the Sahara, sailed the Indian Ocean, traversed the steppes of Central Asia, visited China, and explored the Kingdom of Mali, all within a single lifetime of restless curiosity.

challenges.instruction: Years later he crosses the Sahara to the Mali Empire. Lead the salt caravan south, well to well; each well can be drunk dry only once.
challenges.fact: Ibn Battuta left Tangier in 1325 intending only to make the hajj to Mecca. He was 21 years old. The journey expanded as his curiosity grew — he kept finding reasons not to return home, following trade routes, accepting appointments, and exploring rumors of distant courts. He finally returned to Morocco 29 years later and immediately began planning further travels.

challenges.instruction: The Sultan of Delhi names him envoy to the emperor of China. At Calicut, stow the Sultan’s gifts aboard the junk so she rides level.
challenges.fact: Ibn Battuta's Rihla (A Gift to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities) was dictated to a court secretary, Ibn Juzayy, on his return. Some scholars have questioned whether he visited every place he describes — the China account in particular is suspiciously vague — but his eyewitness descriptions of Mali, India, and Constantinople remain invaluable historical documents.

challenges.instruction: From Constantinople to China, the Mongol peace keeps the roads open. Carry what each city wants and turn a profit along the route.
challenges.fact: The Silk Road was not a single road but a network of shifting routes connecting China to the Mediterranean. Ibn Battuta traveled it in both directions, recording the hospitality of Mongol khans, the luxury of Persian court life, and the stunning efficiency of the Pax Mongolica — the peace imposed by Mongol dominance that made the entire route safe for travelers for the first time.

challenges.instruction: Dictating in Morocco, he remembers the Swahili coast, where he landed at Mombasa and Kilwa in 1331. Play bao against the Zanzibar master and capture the most seeds.
challenges.fact: Ibn Battuta sailed down the Swahili coast in 1331, stopping at Mombasa and Kilwa. He called Kilwa one of the most beautiful and best-built towns in the world, and praised its sultan, known as “the father of gifts” for his generosity.

challenges.instruction: In Fez the scholar Ibn Juzayy writes the travels down and gives the book its title. Decode the words letter by letter.
challenges.fact: The Arabic language was Ibn Battuta's greatest asset. Across the vast arc from Morocco to China, he could walk into any mosque and find educated men who shared his language, his faith, and his legal tradition. The Islamic world of the 14th century was in many ways more unified than any political empire — held together by shared scripture, shared law, and shared script.

challenges.instruction: Lakamha', the city of big water, needs its gardens fed. Open the sluices so water runs down the terraces to every garden — and keep the flood out of the young king's town.
challenges.fact: Pakal became king of Palenque at age 12 in 615 CE and ruled until his death in 683 CE — 68 years on the throne, the longest reign in all of pre-Columbian history. Under his rule, Palenque transformed from a minor city into one of the most powerful and artistically sophisticated kingdoms of the Classic Maya world.

challenges.instruction: The nine terraces of the Temple of the Inscriptions rise stone by stone. Haul each block onto its mark — once a stone is set it cannot be moved again, so raise them in the right order.
challenges.fact: The Temple of the Inscriptions stood in plain sight for centuries — one of Palenque's most prominent structures. But its tomb was not discovered until 1952, when Mexican archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier noticed a stone floor with plugged holes and spent four years clearing a rubble-filled staircase before reaching Pakal's burial chamber 25 metres below.

params.title: The Temple of the Inscriptions
params.intro: Once a limestone block drops onto its terrace mark it is set for good — it can never be pushed off again, or rolled across another mark. Raise the stones in the right order.

challenges.instruction: The Palace astronomers read the sun to time the planting. Plan the milpas year by year so Palenque has maize and beans — and let the tired fields lie fallow.
challenges.fact: The sarcophagus lid of Pakal's tomb shows him at the moment of death, descending into the Maya underworld (Xibalba) on the World Tree. For decades Western scholars misread the image as an astronaut in a spacecraft — a famous case of wishful thinking overriding careful analysis. Maya specialists recognized it as a standard resurrection narrative immediately.

challenges.instruction: Descend the hidden stairway beneath the Temple of the Inscriptions, sealed with rubble for 1,300 years, to the jade king's chamber at the pyramid's heart.
challenges.fact: The staircase descending to Pakal's tomb is 25 metres long and was completely filled with rubble when Alberto Ruz first entered. His team spent four excavation seasons (1949–1952) removing it stone by stone. When they finally broke through the sealed chamber door, they found a jade-encrusted sarcophagus surrounded by six sacrificed retainers and walls painted with the nine lords of the Maya underworld.

challenges.instruction: Deep under the temple, Ruz Lhuillier's crew faces the carved stone lid of Pakal's sarcophagus. Set the fulcrum and the bar so the men can raise the slab high enough to look inside.
challenges.fact: The carved limestone lid of Pakal's sarcophagus measures about 3.8 by 2.2 metres and weighs several tonnes. In November 1952 Ruz's team raised it with jacks and wedged logs beneath it, and saw the king in his jade mask.

challenges.instruction: Pakal's builders tied his tomb to the sky. Find the low winter sun's angle from the shadow it casts across the Palace plaza.
challenges.fact: Maya builders worked without metal tools or draft animals, yet set their monuments to the sky. Linda Schele noted in the 1970s that, seen from the Palace, the sun at the winter solstice sets directly behind the Temple of the Inscriptions — as if the dying sun were entering Pakal's tomb.

params.title: The Solstice Sun at Palenque
params.goal: Drag the setting sun until the 2 m stela casts a shadow exactly 10 m long. Only the sun's angle above the horizon is shown.
params.explanation: tan θ = 2/10 → θ ≈ 11.3°. Maya astronomers followed the sun's path through the year; seen from the Palace at Palenque, the winter-solstice sun sets behind the Temple of the Inscriptions.
