params.title: Out of the Burning Capital
params.intro: Kyoto, summer 1183: the Minamoto close in. The child emperor cannot fight — he cannot help take a raider, not even as the far side of a sandwich. Your four guards must do all the fighting while he runs for a corner.
params.fact: When the Taira abandoned Kyoto in the seventh month of 1183, they took the five-year-old Emperor Antoku and the three sacred regalia with them, so that wherever the clan went, the throne went too.

challenges.instruction: While the clan escorts the boy emperor out of Kyoto, Tadanori turns back alone toward Shunzei’s gate. Guard the emperor’s flight and get him clear of the closing ring.
challenges.fact: Tadanori was one of the leading waka poets of his generation, a student of the master Fujiwara no Shunzei. On the eve of the Taira clan's final flight from Kyoto, he rode back alone through the night to deliver a scroll of his poems to Shunzei — asking only that one be included in the imperial anthology. One was: it appears in the Senzai Wakashū without his name, since he died a rebel.

challenges.instruction: The Taira take to their ships and the Minamoto hold every harbour mouth. Shift the crowding boats aside and steer the imperial vessel out to open water.
challenges.fact: Because Tadanori died on the losing side of the Genpei War, his poem was included in the Senzai Wakashū as 'anonymous' — it would have been politically unacceptable to honor a Taira rebel by name. Yet the poem's inclusion was itself an act of aesthetic respect. Everyone knew whose poem it was, and that silent knowledge became part of the poem's beauty.

params.title: Fukuhara Abandoned, 1183
params.rule: Burn the stores, spare the quay
params.intro: The Minamoto are coming. Torch houses so the wind carries the fire through every storehouse (🌾) before they arrive, and pull down houses so it never reaches the stone quay (🏰). You have fewer torches than storehouses.

challenges.instruction: In 1183 the Taira abandon the capital, then Fukuhara, the port Kiyomori built for the ships of Song China. Leave nothing for the Minamoto: let the wind carry fire through the storehouses, and keep it off the stone quay where the fleet waits.
challenges.fact: The tale of Tadanori riding back to his poetry master on the night of defeat became one of the most celebrated stories in Japanese literary history. It appears in the Heike Monogatari — the great narrative of the Genpei War — as the moment when a warrior reveals that poetry, not victory, is what he cannot bear to leave behind.

challenges.instruction: Tadanori’s killer unties a paper from the fallen warrior’s quiver. Read the poem shape by shape and learn whose life he has taken.
challenges.fact: The Heike Monogatari opens with the most famous line in Japanese literature: 'The sound of the Gion Shoja bells echoes the impermanence of all things.' It was not read but performed — chanted to biwa accompaniment by traveling monks who served as medieval Japan's living archive of history and loss.

challenges.instruction: Years later Shunzei unrolls the scroll Tadanori left at his gate. Find the roller that lines up the words and read how the anthology will name him.
challenges.fact: The Battle of Ichi-no-Tani (1184) was a Minamoto tactical masterpiece: while one force engaged the Taira from the front, Minamoto Yoshitsune led cavalry down a cliff believed to be impassable. The surprise attack from above broke the Taira position. Tadanori died fighting in this rout — killed by a Minamoto warrior who recognized him only by a poem tucked inside his armour.

params.title: Dan-no-ura, 1185
params.intro: In the strait the Taira ships keep moving: each turn every ship moves one square along its row, turning about at the shore. You cannot see them — until one is hit and burns.

challenges.instruction: Spring 1185: the last Taira fleet meets the Minamoto in the strait of Dan-no-ura, where the tide runs hard and turns at midday. The ships never stop moving with the current. Find them before the day is spent.
challenges.fact: At Dan-no-ura, in the Kanmon Strait, the Taira fleet was destroyed on 25 April 1185. As the battle turned, Kiyomori's widow leapt into the sea with the child emperor Antoku in her arms, and the clan Tadanori died for was gone.

challenges.instruction: The Yoshioka school has gathered its whole following under the pine at Ichijō-ji to finish the stranger. Slide the ranks aside and cut a way out.
challenges.fact: By his own count Musashi fought more than sixty duels before he was thirty and never lost one. The Yoshioka fights of 1604 in Kyoto made his name.

challenges.instruction: Musashi teaches that one Way runs through every art — the sword, the brush, even a game of stones. Read the board as you would an opponent and line up five first.
challenges.fact: Musashi never lost a duel in 60+ fights. In his later years he renounced killing, became a painter and sculptor, and wrote The Book of Five Rings — still read by business leaders and martial artists worldwide.

challenges.instruction: Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, Void: Musashi sees his strategy in everything, and he paints as he fights. In Kyoto his contemporary Tawaraya Sōtatsu painted the gods of wind and thunder on gold. Restore their colours.
challenges.fact: Musashi arrived late for his duel with Kojiro on Ganryūjima island (1612), having carved a practice sword from a boat oar on the way. He killed Kojiro with one strike — the psychological warfare of his lateness was as devastating as the blow.

challenges.instruction: In a cave on Mount Iwato an old swordsman writes down all he knows. Put the opening of The Book of Five Rings back in order.
challenges.fact: Musashi was also one of the finest ink painters of his age: works such as Shrike on a Withered Branch are Important Cultural Properties of Japan.

challenges.instruction: Bellini's workshop still talks of the German who came to Venice, Albrecht Dürer. Complete the magic square he would later engrave: every line, every quarter, the centre and the corners.
challenges.fact: Albrecht Dürer stayed in Venice in 1505–07 and wrote home that the aged Giovanni Bellini, Titian's master, was still the best painter of them all. His engraving Melencolia I, with its magic square, followed in 1514.

challenges.instruction: Master Titian's Assumption of the Virgin has lost its colour. Find the right pigments for the Virgin's mantle and dress, as Titian painted them.
challenges.fact: Venetian painting was distinguished by its rich colour, applied in multiple glazed layers over days or weeks. Titian's reds — sometimes called 'Titian red' — were achieved with expensive vermilion and glazes of lake pigment.

challenges.instruction: Titian's Venice was famous for its madrigals. Arrange notes of a Renaissance vocal phrase — the music Titian heard daily.
challenges.fact: Venice's Basilica di San Marco had two organ lofts facing each other, inspiring the 'cori spezzati' style — antiphonal music where choirs answer each other across space. Giovanni Gabrieli developed this into orchestral writing.

challenges.instruction: In Titian's last years his friend Daniele Barbaro teaches painters a new trick: a lens in the wall of a darkened room. Open the wall so each candle's image falls on its mark.
challenges.fact: Barbaro's camera used a convex lens, the kind Venice's spectacle-makers ground, to throw an image bright enough to trace. Titian, still painting in his eighties, died in Venice in August 1576 during an outbreak of plague.

challenges.instruction: Paint each section of the bowl with the right metal oxide glaze before firing.
challenges.fact: Venetian glassmakers on Murano pioneered cobalt blue glass using smalt — cobalt oxide imported from Saxony — becoming the dominant blue pigment in Renaissance Europe.

challenges.instruction: Bid on rare Renaissance goods at the Rialto Auction House. Win the starred items before your budget runs out.
challenges.fact: Venice's Rialto market was one of Europe's first commodity exchanges, trading silk, spices, and art from across the known world.

challenges.instruction: Titian painted at breakneck speed. Reassemble the fragments of his Assumption of the Virgin — fit the pieces together until the composition is whole.
challenges.fact: Titian's Assumption of the Virgin (1518) shattered every convention of Renaissance altarpiece painting. The Cardinal of Venice initially refused to accept it — then stood speechless before it.

challenges.instruction: You are the new curator of the Uffizi. Assign each Renaissance masterpiece to the room where it earns the greatest bonus and hit the target score.
challenges.fact: The Uffizi Gallery in Florence holds the finest concentration of Renaissance masterpieces in the world — Botticelli's Venus, da Vinci's Annunciation, and Titian's Venus of Urbino under one roof.

challenges.instruction: The ancient marbles that taught Venice's painters are being catalogued for the Republic. Recover each piece from the damp-stained inventory.
challenges.fact: Titian's St Sebastian in the Averoldi altarpiece (1520–22) borrows the twisting pose of the Laocoön, the ancient marble rediscovered in Rome in 1506. Venetian painters learned from antiquities as eagerly as the Florentines.

challenges.instruction: Before the five ships leave Seville, their holds must carry what the Spice Islands will take in trade for cloves. Stow the barter goods worth the most and leave the dead weight on the quay.
challenges.fact: Only 18 men completed the first circumnavigation, arriving back in Spain in September 1522 — three years after departing. Magellan himself was killed in the Philippines in April 1521, so he never finished the journey.

challenges.instruction: Sort each port or landmark into the ocean Magellan's fleet crossed to reach it.
challenges.fact: Magellan named the Pacific Ocean 'Mar Pacífico' — the peaceful sea — after the violent storms of the strait that now bears his name. The irony was that the Pacific crossing nearly killed his crew from starvation.

challenges.instruction: At Tidore the survivors could buy fresh fruit at last, after scurvy had killed many of them on the Pacific crossing. Titrate a lime’s juice with alkali and stop at the endpoint to measure its citric acid.
challenges.fact: At Tidore in November 1521 the two surviving ships, Trinidad and Victoria, took on cloves. The Trinidad sprang a leak and stayed behind for repairs; only the Victoria, under Juan Sebastián Elcano, sailed on west for Spain.

challenges.instruction: Elcano brings the Victoria home the long way, round Africa and clear of the Portuguese. Buy and sell at every landfall so the cargo is worth the lives it cost.
challenges.fact: The Victoria's cloves sold in Spain for more than the cost of the whole expedition. Charles V gave Elcano a coat of arms bearing a globe and the motto Primus circumdedisti me — 'You first went around me.'

challenges.instruction: The great lords of Castile will not bow to a queen of twenty-three. Beat them at their own game on the old Castilian board: form mills, take their pieces and leave them no line to hold.
challenges.fact: Isabel's claim to Castile was contested by her niece Juana, backed by Afonso V of Portugal and many of the great nobles. The War of the Castilian Succession turned at Toro in 1476 and ended with the Treaty of Alcáçovas in 1479.

challenges.instruction: Granada falls in January 1492, and the Alhambra is Isabel's. Set one queen in every glaze of its tilework — one per row, column and colour, and none touching.
challenges.fact: On 2 January 1492 Muhammad XII, the last Nasrid sultan, handed the keys of Granada to Isabel and Ferdinand, ending nearly eight centuries of Muslim rule in Iberia. That April, at Santa Fe outside the city, they signed the agreement that sent Columbus west.

challenges.instruction: Queen Isabel must build a court coalition to fund Columbus's westward voyage. The treasury is drained — choose which concessions to grant so enough factions back the plan.
challenges.fact: The Capitulations of Santa Fe (1492) gave Columbus the title of Admiral and a share of profits. Isabel's gamble yielded the largest territorial windfall in European history.

challenges.instruction: Isabel's gamble pays: Columbus has found land across the Ocean Sea. Ride the trade winds west from the Canaries, then swing north to the westerlies to bring the news home to Castile.
challenges.fact: On his first voyage in 1492 Columbus sailed south to the Canaries to pick up the north-east trade winds, and in 1493 he came home far to the north, on the westerlies. Spanish fleets followed the same loop for three centuries.

challenges.instruction: In Salamanca a chess book is printed for Isabel's son and heir. Follow the knight's path it sets — every square once, the numbered squares in order.
challenges.fact: Prince Juan, to whom Lucena dedicated his chess book, died in October 1497 at nineteen. The crowns of Castile and Aragon passed through his sister Juana to her son, the future Emperor Charles V.

challenges.instruction: Manuel's council warns that a fleet to India will ruin the kingdom. Win the court round, faction by faction, before the ships can sail.
challenges.fact: 'Manuel, o Venturoso' — The Fortunate. Under his reign, Vasco da Gama reached India (1498), Pedro Cabral reached Brazil (1500), and Portugal controlled the world's spice trade. Lisbon became the richest city in Europe.

challenges.instruction: Calicut's ruler will not let the newcomers stay. Hold the fords of Cochin, Portugal's only ally, with a handful of men against his army.
challenges.fact: Vasco da Gama's first voyage of 1497–99 lost two of its four ships and more than half its men, but the spices it brought home paid for it many times over. Manuel answered Calicut's hostility with armed fleets every year and a chain of forts.

challenges.instruction: With Goa, Malacca and Hormuz in Portuguese hands, the riches of the East come up the Tagus. Reckon each cargo into the king's ledger as the clerk calls it.
challenges.fact: Albuquerque took Goa in 1510, Malacca in 1511 and Hormuz in 1515, giving Portugal command of the straits of the Indian Ocean. For a generation Lisbon set the price of pepper for all of Europe.

challenges.instruction: From Lisbon to Malacca, Manuel's forts ring the Indian Ocean, and in their shadow life goes on. Sit down at the board with a merchant of Kilwa.
challenges.fact: Manuel's reign gave its name to the Manueline style, whose stone ropes, armillary spheres and sea creatures cover the Jerónimos Monastery and the Tower of Belém in Lisbon, both built with the profits of the spice trade.

challenges.instruction: Not all of Manuel's fortune comes from the East: Madeira's sugar mills grind for the crown too. Build the gear train so the water wheel turns the crushing stone just right.
challenges.fact: Madeira, settled by the Portuguese from the 1420s, was Europe's great source of sugar by 1500. The planters' methods were carried on to São Tomé and then to Brazil, the land Cabral claimed for Manuel in 1500.

challenges.fact: A Local Survival event is a test, not a fight: at the end of each round every side at the location is checked, and a total under 5 loses every card there to the discard pile. Reinforce with followers, or retrieve a weak card before the round ends.

challenges.instruction: From Toungoo, Bayinnaung sets out to make himself king of kings. Carry the realms from Ava to Ayutthaya before Siam's king can rally them against you.
challenges.fact: Bayinnaung (1516–1581) built the largest empire in Southeast Asian history, conquering the Shan States, the Lan Na kingdom (Chiang Mai), and twice capturing Ayutthaya (the Siamese capital). His Toungoo Empire briefly unified Burma, Thailand, Laos, and portions of Yunnan under one administration.

challenges.instruction: Bayinnaung lets the kings he defeats keep their thrones — if they swear to him. Seat one sworn king in every realm, with no two close enough to plot together.
challenges.fact: Bayinnaung was known for remarkable religious tolerance. He allowed conquered rulers to keep their thrones as vassals, permitted local customs to continue, and interfered with Portuguese missionaries in Pegu only when they destroyed Buddhist temples. He sought legitimacy through ceremony and generosity as much as through force.

challenges.instruction: Merchants from China, India and Portugal crowd the ports of Pegu. Trade along the coast and up the river, and make the King of Kings' ports the richest on the Bay of Bengal.
challenges.fact: The white elephant was the ultimate symbol of royal legitimacy in Southeast Asia. When Bayinnaung captured Ayutthaya's white elephants, he was claiming the spiritual mandate of regional kingship. His Pegu capital became one of the most cosmopolitan cities in Asia, hosting Portuguese traders, Siamese princes, and Chinese merchants simultaneously.

challenges.instruction: With no roads through the jungle, Bayinnaung moves his host by water. Bring the war boats up the Irrawaddy past the sandbanks and snags to the camp at Ava.
challenges.fact: Bayinnaung's military campaigns required extraordinary logistical sophistication — moving armies through tropical jungle with no road infrastructure. He developed a system of river transport, local supply contracts, and staged advance bases that would not have been out of place in a modern campaign.

challenges.instruction: Pegu's markets traded silks, rubies, elephants, and spices with Portuguese merchants and Chinese fleets. Match the commodities that flow through the greatest emporium of Southeast Asia.
challenges.fact: The city of Pegu under Bayinnaung was described by the Portuguese merchant Fernão Mendes Pinto as the most magnificent city he had ever seen — and he had visited Malacca, Goa, and Hormuz. Its markets brought together goods from China, India, the Spice Islands, and Europe in a single magnificent bazaar.

challenges.instruction: Bayinnaung's treasury runs on tribute, tolls and the ruby trade, and every campaign costs more than the last. Buy and sell the stones through the seasons and fill the treasury before the next war.
challenges.fact: Bayinnaung's empire was as much a trade network as a military conquest. Control of the overland route between China and the Indian Ocean gave his treasury a cut of the most profitable commerce in Asia. The Portuguese paid handsomely for port rights in Pegu — and Bayinnaung collected from everyone.

challenges.instruction: Copying a book takes a monk a year, and old copyists' eyes fail by candlelight. Before Gutenberg changes how books are made, help them see: bring each candle's image to its mark.
challenges.fact: Gutenberg's breakthrough was casting individual metal letters that could be arranged, printed, and rearranged indefinitely. The same 26 letters (in his case Gothic type) could print any text in any order — unlike woodblocks, which could only print the single text carved into them. His oil-based ink and screw press were important innovations, but the movable metal type was the revolution.

challenges.instruction: Fust's money is in the workshop, and the Bible of 42 lines must be set page by page. Compose the forme — mirrored, right to left — then ink it and pull the press.
challenges.fact: The 42-line Bible was finished at Mainz by 1455. About 180 copies were printed, some on vellum and most on paper; 49 survive, complete or in part.

challenges.instruction: Fust sues and takes the press. In this puzzle a note in a grid code records how the inventor ended his days — match each shape to its letter and read it.
challenges.fact: Gutenberg died nearly broke. His primary financial backer, Johann Fust, sued him over unpaid loans and won — seizing the printing equipment and the first run of Bibles. The press that changed the world made little money for its inventor. Gutenberg was awarded a pension by the Archbishop of Mainz in his final years, dying in 1468 largely unrewarded by the revolution he had started.

challenges.instruction: In 1462 Mainz is sacked, and its printers scatter, taking the craft with them. Get one printer's household and goods across the Rhine.
challenges.fact: It took 50 years for printing to reach every corner of Europe. By 1500, over 20 million books had been printed — more than all the manuscripts produced in the previous thousand years of European history. The printing press did not merely copy existing knowledge; it transformed who could access it, who could challenge it, and who could add to it.

challenges.instruction: Every book and every newspaper owes him a debt — even the ancients' secrets are in print now. Wind the strip on the right rod and read what his invention means.
challenges.fact: Gutenberg never put his name on a book. Most of what we know of his work comes from lawsuits and loan records — above all the Helmasperger notarial instrument of 1455, which records Fust's suit against him.

challenges.instruction: In 1592 the beacon fires blaze along the coast: the Japanese have landed. Read the alarm as it runs from tower to tower — each letter a row and a column of the square.
challenges.fact: The turtle ship (geobukseon) was the world's first ironclad warship — its curved, iron-plated deck prevented Japanese boarding parties from swarming the deck in their preferred hand-to-hand style. It carried cannons on all sides and a dragon's head at the bow that could emit smoke to disorient the enemy. Yi deployed it as a spearhead to break enemy formations before his lighter warships engaged.

challenges.instruction: Before Hansan, Yi plots his patrols through the islands like the horse on a janggi board. Visit every point once and come home to where you began.
challenges.fact: The Battle of Hansan Island (1592) is considered one of the most significant naval battles in Asian history. Yi used a feigned retreat to draw the Japanese fleet into open water, then sprang the crane-wing encirclement. He sank 47 Japanese ships and captured 12, breaking Japan's naval dominance in a single afternoon.

challenges.instruction: Stripped of rank and serving as a common soldier, Yi still thinks in lines and formations. Play the camp's board game — every line of three takes a piece.
challenges.fact: Yi was arrested, tortured, and demoted twice — the victim of court intrigue and a Japanese deception operation that planted false intelligence to undermine him. He served as a common soldier before being hastily reinstated when the navy collapsed without him. Myeongnyang was fought with the 13 ships that remained after his absence.

challenges.instruction: Korean resistance against invasion required total commitment. Command the naval engagement — read the current, hold the strait, and let geography be your fleet.
challenges.fact: At Myeongnyang in 1597, Admiral Yi commanded just 13 remaining warships against a Japanese fleet of over 300. He positioned his ships in the narrow strait where the current reversed twice daily, luring the Japanese into a bottleneck where numbers meant nothing. He sank or damaged 31 enemy ships without losing a single one of his own.

challenges.instruction: At Hansan Island, Yi surrounded the Japanese fleet using the 'Crane Wing' formation — a classic envelopment. Execute the maneuver: extend the wings, close the trap, allow no escape.
challenges.fact: Yi Sun-sin died at Noryang in 1598 — struck by a bullet during the battle that would finally expel Japanese forces from Korea. His last words, reportedly, were: 'The battle is at its height — do not announce my death.' He won the battle from his deathbed, concealing his death until the Japanese had fled.

challenges.instruction: Yi studied Sun Tzu as carefully as he studied tides. Deploy your forces where terrain, timing, and surprise multiply every ship's effectiveness.
challenges.fact: Yi's battle reports, collected in his Nanjung Ilgi (War Diary), are among the most detailed military documents of the 16th century. He recorded his tactics, his anxieties, his observations of weather and tide, and his grief. The diary survived the war hidden under floorboards. It is now a Korean national treasure.

challenges.instruction: Tenochtitlan feeds 200,000 people from gardens built out into the lake. Plan the chinampa fields season by season to bring in the maize.
challenges.fact: Tenochtitlan, built on an island in Lake Texcoco, was one of the largest cities in the world in 1500 — home to 200,000–300,000 people, larger than London, Paris, or any city in Spain. When Hernán Cortés' soldiers first saw it, they wrote that they thought they were dreaming. Its causeways, aqueducts, and floating gardens had no parallel in European experience.

challenges.instruction: Tribute pours in from every province — gold, jade, jaguar skins, and bags of cochineal from Oaxaca. Mix the crimson the tribute dye makes.
challenges.fact: Montezuma II pushed the empire's wars south into Oaxaca and east toward the Gulf coast. The great Sun Stone, now usually dated to his reign, was dug up beneath Mexico City's main square in 1790.

challenges.instruction: Strangers have landed on the coast in floating houses. Montezuma's envoys bring their report in paint, as Mexica scribes always had. Restore a page those scribes painted twenty years later: the founding of Tenochtitlan.
challenges.fact: The story that Montezuma mistook Cortés for Quetzalcoatl appears in later accounts heavily influenced by Spanish interpreters and indigenous collaborators with reasons to justify the conquest. Modern historians believe Montezuma was an experienced and politically sophisticated ruler who recognized the Spanish as dangerous strangers — not gods. He attempted to manage the threat diplomatically before it overwhelmed him.

challenges.instruction: Montezuma is a hostage in his own palace, and after the massacre the city rises. The warriors take up the canal bridges to trap the Spaniards — lift or lay as few as you must so a runner can still cross every one.
challenges.fact: The conquest of the Aztec Empire was not a European conquest of indigenous people — it was a coalition war. Cortés' key allies, the Tlaxcalans, had been enemies of the Aztec Triple Alliance for generations and contributed far more warriors to the siege of Tenochtitlan than the Spanish did. The Aztec empire fell to its own enemies as much as to European weapons.

challenges.instruction: Montezuma reportedly drank fifty cups of cacao daily from golden cups — the drink of emperors. Prepare the xocolatl as the palace kitchens did: bitter, spiced, and served cold.
challenges.fact: Cacao was the currency and the luxury of the Aztec world simultaneously — you could pay your taxes with it, or drink it if you were noble enough. The xocolatl the Aztecs drank was nothing like modern chocolate: it was ground cacao mixed with water, vanilla, chili, and achiote, beaten to a foam and served cold. The Spanish found it revolting at first, then addictive.

challenges.instruction: The empire falls, but the markets Cortés marvelled at were stocked by merchants who walked. Lead the porters' line to every load the Tlatelolco market has ordered.
challenges.fact: The Spanish soldier Bernal Díaz del Castillo wrote that the Tlatelolco market was 'like the squares of Salamanca, but twice as big, crowded with people, and more orderly.' It traded everything: food, textiles, gold, slaves, feathers, medicine, and pottery. Every item had a fixed price and market inspectors enforced fair trading.

challenges.fact: A Local Survival event is a test, not a fight: at the end of each round every side at the location is checked, and a total under 5 loses every card there to the discard pile. Reinforce with followers, or retrieve a weak card before the round ends.

challenges.instruction: Before the Spanish can reach Quito, Rumiñahui's cord keepers must count what is to be hidden. Read only the cords of the colour asked — yellow for gold, red for warriors — and give him the total.
challenges.fact: Rumiñahui ('Stone Eye') was Atahualpa's most capable general. When Pizarro captured and executed the Inca emperor in 1533, Rumiñahui gathered the northern army and led resistance from Quito. Rather than let Pizarro's forces loot the city's treasures, he burned Quito and hid its gold — a legendary hoard that has never been found.

challenges.instruction: Belalcázar's horsemen are coming up the road. Rumiñahui's warriors have hidden pits across the plain — bring your own men through without falling into one.
challenges.fact: Belalcázar marched on Quito in 1534 with about 200 Spaniards and thousands of Cañari and other native allies who hated Atahualpa's rule. Rumiñahui fought them at Teocajas and in the passes for months before falling back on the city.

challenges.instruction: Quito will burn rather than become a Spanish trophy — but first its treasure must go. Lead the llama train to each load before the Spanish arrive, then on into the mountains.
challenges.fact: The lost treasure of Quito became one of the great legends of the Americas. Expeditions searched for it for centuries, and legends of El Dorado were partly inspired by the belief that Rumiñahui had hidden an incomprehensible fortune somewhere in the Andes. No credible discovery has ever been made.

challenges.instruction: The Spanish close in from every side. Rumiñahui's bands fall back through the gorges, cutting each rope bridge behind them — find the line of retreat that crosses every bridge exactly once.
challenges.fact: The Spanish advantage in the Inca conquest was not just steel and gunpowder — it was horses. The Inca had no large domesticated animals. The sight of mounted soldiers, armored in steel, was psychologically devastating. Rumiñahui understood this and consistently drew Spanish forces into terrain that negated the horse — steep trails, forest, and fast rivers.

challenges.instruction: Rumiñahui is gone, but the roads he fought along remain. Run the message through every post of the Inca road and home again, as the chasquis did.
challenges.fact: The Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road network of some 30,000 km, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014, shared by six countries from Colombia to Chile — Ecuador among them.

challenges.instruction: The Spanish will forbid the feast of the Sun and put out its fires. Kindle the last fire as the priests did at Inti Raymi, bringing the light to a single point.
challenges.fact: Rumiñahui was executed in Quito in 1535. Ecuador honours him as a national hero of indigenous resistance, and a canton near Quito bears his name.

challenges.instruction: Maxtla's Tepanecs mean to starve the Mexica into submission. Hold the island city while Tlacaelel binds Texcoco and Tlacopan into an alliance.
challenges.fact: Tlacaelel (c.1397–1487) held the office of Cihuacoatl — officially the second speaker, the emperor's shadow. In practice, he directed state policy under three emperors (Itzcoatl, Motecuhzoma I, and Axayacatl) for over fifty years. He was offered the supreme throne three times and refused it each time — understanding that the power behind the throne is more durable than the throne itself.

challenges.instruction: Tlacaelel will not take the throne, but he steers every emperor who does. After the great flood of 1449, bring the tribute canoes through the gates of the new dike.
challenges.fact: Tlacaelel served as cihuacoatl under Itzcoatl, Motecuhzoma I and Axayacatl. Chronicles describe Motecuhzoma I and Tlacaelel ruling almost as a pair, and the great waterworks of the mid-1400s — the dike across the lake, the aqueduct from Chapultepec — date from their time.

challenges.instruction: Tlacaelel has the old painted histories burned. Restore the page of the new one: the eagle on the cactus in the lake.
challenges.fact: Tlacaelel ordered the burning of existing historical codices — the painted books that recorded Aztec history before his reforms. He then commissioned new histories that placed the Mexica at the center of a divinely ordained cosmic narrative. The burning was not destruction for its own sake: it was the replacement of one story with a more useful one.

challenges.instruction: The Flower Wars begin — battles fixed by agreement and fought to take captives for the gods. March the warriors out to the beat of the drums.
challenges.fact: The Flower Wars (Xochiyaoyotl) that Tlacaelel institutionalized were a unique form of ritualized conflict: neighboring states would agree to scheduled battles whose purpose was not territorial conquest but the capture of living warriors for sacrifice. Critics called them morally monstrous; defenders argued they were a more humane alternative to wars of annihilation. The truth is that they also kept potential rivals permanently weak.

challenges.instruction: Tlacaelel governed through persuasion as much as power. Present your policy to the council of lords — frame the war as cosmic necessity, the sacrifice as divine service, the conquest as salvation.
challenges.fact: The Aztec ruling council (tlatocan) included leaders of the Triple Alliance's three cities and was theoretically a collective body. Tlacaelel's genius was making its decisions feel consensual while ensuring they reflected his vision. He was a master of what modern political scientists call 'agenda control' — determining not just how issues were decided but which issues were ever discussed.

challenges.instruction: In 1455 a 52-year cycle ends and every fire in the valley goes out. On the Hill of the Star, follow the wandering light until it comes all the way round — and the world goes on.
challenges.fact: Tlacaelel's greatest achievement was ideological: he transformed the Mexica from one of many Nahua-speaking peoples into the chosen people of the sun god, with a cosmic obligation to feed Huitzilopochtli through human sacrifice. This narrative made every war a religious act and every conquest a divine duty — creating the psychological engine that drove Aztec expansion for a century.

challenges.instruction: Robert lodges with Friedrich Wieck and practises to his teacher's strict beat. Pick out every pendulum that keeps time with the reference — the discipline Florestan hates and Eusebius needs.
challenges.fact: Schumann's Florestan (passionate extrovert) and Eusebius (dreaming introvert) represented the two sides of Romantic temperament. He used both names in his music journal Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, which he founded in 1834.

challenges.instruction: Clara is a child prodigy who already writes her own music. Put the notes of her rising Romantic phrase in order.
challenges.fact: Clara Schumann (1819–1896) gave her first public performance at age nine and her last at seventy-one. She performed across Europe for over sixty years, premiering works by her husband Robert and her closest friend Johannes Brahms. Brahms said: 'Clara is the most gifted artist and personality I have ever known.'
In 1839 Clara toured Paris without her father. That summer she and Robert went to court in Leipzig to marry without Wieck's consent; the judges ruled for them in August 1840.
challenges.instruction: In 1839 Clara goes to Paris without her father to play on her own terms. Read the notice in Louis Braille's raised dots, the code taught at the city's school for the blind, one letter at a time.
Robert writes the songs; Clara carries them from city to city. Lay her line from Leipzig to Vienna through every concert town in order, with as few curves as you can.
challenges.fact: Schumann championed young talent — he was one of the first critics to recognise Chopin and Brahms publicly. His review of Brahms' debut announced: 'a young eagle has arrived.' Brahms was twenty, Schumann forty-three.

challenges.instruction: With Robert in Endenich, Clara must keep seven children, her concerts and his name from colliding. Place every queen so that none of them threatens another.
challenges.fact: With Robert confined at Endenich from March 1854, the twenty-year-old Johannes Brahms moved to Düsseldorf to help Clara and the children, while she went back on tour to support the family. The eight queens puzzle had been posed by the Bavarian chess composer Max Bezzel in the Berliner Schachzeitung in 1848.

challenges.instruction: In July 1856 a telegram comes from Endenich. Read the dots and dashes and learn what Clara must do.
challenges.fact: Robert Schumann died at the Endenich asylum near Bonn on 29 July 1856, aged 46. Clara had reached him two days earlier; she wrote that he knew her and put his arm around her.

challenges.instruction: Brahms, Clara's closest friend after Robert's death, finished his German Requiem in 1868. Put its movements in the order he wrote them.
challenges.fact: Brahms was devoted to Clara for the rest of her life. She championed his music from his first compositions, and he dedicated works to her memory. Their 40-year friendship was the great sustaining relationship of both their lives.

challenges.instruction: Fight lesson 5 · Face Down. Win two attacks: fight at London where the Art Critique is running, then carry the fight to Moscow by starting your own event there.
challenges.fact: A card on the board can be public (face up) or private (face down). A private card hides its identity and stats from rivals until an attack reveals every card at that location. Your own cards deploy face down; Go Public when being seen helps you.

challenges.question: Linnaeus classified approximately how many species in his lifetime?
challenges.fact: Linnaeus formally described and classified about 12,000 species — roughly 6,000 plants and 6,000 animals. His two-part naming system (genus + species) is still used today for over 1.8 million known species.

challenges.instruction: Classify each organism into Linnaeus's kingdoms.
challenges.fact: Linnaeus created the system we still use today. His binomial names — like Homo sapiens — gave every species a unique two-word Latin identity understood by scientists worldwide.

challenges.instruction: Linnaeus will print what the bones tell him, whatever the bishops say. Set the type for the tenth edition of Systema Naturae, where humankind takes its new name.
challenges.fact: Linnaeus classified 7,700 plant species and 4,400 animal species. His binomial system — genus plus species — replaced unwieldy Latin phrases with clean two-word names still used by every scientist on Earth. Naming Homo sapiens was audacious: placing humanity inside the animal kingdom challenged centuries of theological certainty.

challenges.instruction: Back in Uppsala, Linnaeus lays out the university garden as a living Systema Naturae. Plant the trees so that no two share a row, column or diagonal.
challenges.fact: Linnaeus first set humans beside the apes in 1735 and named us Homo sapiens in 1758. Critics were outraged; in a 1747 letter to the botanist Johann Gmelin he wrote that he knew of no generic difference between man and ape that followed from the principles of natural history.

challenges.instruction: Linnaeus's student Pehr Osbeck sails as chaplain on a Swedish East Indiaman, collecting plants for his teacher. Bring the ship into Canton on the summer monsoon and home again on the winter one, specimens and all.
challenges.fact: Linnaeus sent some seventeen students — his 'apostles' — round the world: Osbeck to China, Hasselquist to the Levant, Forsskål to Arabia, Solander with Cook to Australia, Thunberg to Japan. Several died on the road, but the specimens they sent back made Linnaean names the common language of naturalists everywhere.

params.title: Osbeck Sails for Canton, 1751

Louis XVI became king at nineteen on 10 May 1774, when his grandfather Louis XV died of smallpox, inheriting a state close to bankruptcy. He was a skilled locksmith and a passionate map-maker — a careful craftsman in a role that demanded bold political vision.

params.plaintext: THE KING IS DEAD LONG LIVE THE KING

challenges.instruction: Louis remembers May 1774, when a note in the courtiers' grid code ran through Versailles as his grandfather lay dead. Read it — the words that made a nineteen-year-old king.

Once the Estates-General meet, news from Versailles outruns every courier. Plan the line of signal towers the Chappe brothers would soon propose, so that every city of France can see the next one's arms.
challenges.fact: The Palace of Versailles was a machine of political spectacle — every corridor, mirror, and gilded surface designed to awe visitors into submission. Louis XVI inherited this stage but never fully commanded it.

challenges.instruction: It is July 1789. The Bastille has fallen. Louis XVI needs enough of the Estates behind him to keep his crown — choose the concessions that hold a coalition together.
challenges.fact: Louis XVI was guillotined on 21 January 1793, convicted of treason. His fatal error — the Flight to Varennes in June 1791 — proved to the Revolutionary government that he was conspiring against France with foreign powers.

challenges.instruction: When the factions will not obey him, Louis retreats to the one machine he understands: his locksmith's bench. Set the gates so the lock's levers agree with the table on every row.
challenges.fact: Louis XVI kept a locksmith's forge above his private apartments at Versailles and worked there with the locksmith François Gamain. In November 1792 Gamain revealed the hidden iron cupboard, the armoire de fer, that he had helped the king fit in the Tuileries; its papers were used against Louis at his trial.

challenges.instruction: Before Siccar Point, Hutton had found the same broken join at Jedburgh, and his friend John Clerk drew it. Piece the drawing back together and see what he saw: flat sandstone laid across layers stood on end.
challenges.fact: James Hutton (1726–1797) is called the 'Father of Modern Geology' for his Theory of the Earth (1788), which proposed that the Earth's features were shaped by slow, ongoing natural processes — not a single catastrophic event.

challenges.instruction: Playfair is right that the critics are coming. Defend the Theory of the Earth against Richard Kirwan with the evidence of the rocks, not with defiance.
challenges.fact: The geological timescale assembled during and after Hutton's lifetime required his key insight: processes we observe today — erosion, deposition, volcanism — are the same ones that shaped ancient rocks. If the present is the key to the past, the past must be unimaginably long.

challenges.instruction: Hutton holds that the Earth renews itself the way the planets keep their courses — and in 1759 Halley's comet came back exactly as foretold. Set the comet's speed so it returns on time, the kind of law Hutton wants for rocks.
challenges.fact: Hutton realised that the volume of sediment deposited in river deltas must equal the volume of rock eroded from mountains — and that the mountains were still there. The rates of erosion he could observe were so slow that the cycle must have repeated millions of times. Geometry became an argument for deep time.

challenges.instruction: Hutton was a farmer before he was a geologist, and the soil taught him that the Earth feeds itself. Run his Norfolk rotation so every field keeps yielding, year after year, with none left to rest.
challenges.fact: Hutton's 1788 paper 'Theory of the Earth' proposed that the planet was a self-maintaining system — soil feeds plants, erosion renews the soil, uplift renews the mountains. This 'steady-state' Earth anticipated modern geology and ecology by two centuries. James Lovelock's Gaia hypothesis of 1972 owes an explicit debt to Hutton.

challenges.instruction: "It is a machine," Hutton says. Build his machine in miniature: gear the water-wheel to the millstone so it turns true, as rivers, seas and fire turn the Earth.
challenges.fact: Darwin read Lyell's Principles of Geology on the HMS Beagle and was transformed by it. The logic — that gradual, uniform processes over immense time can produce dramatic change — applies equally to geology and to evolution. Darwin acknowledged: 'The idea that geology had done for rocks, I wished to do for species.' Hutton's deep time was the foundation Darwin needed.

challenges.instruction: Queen Charlotte's order has made Wedgwood's cream-coloured ware the fashion. Carry the stack of dishes to the packing bench one at a time, never a larger on a smaller — a single broken piece shames the 'Potter to Her Majesty'.
challenges.fact: Josiah Wedgwood didn't just make pottery — he invented modern manufacturing. He introduced quality control, a money-back guarantee, free delivery, and celebrity endorsements. His factory pioneered the division of labour decades before Adam Smith wrote about it.

challenges.instruction: Thousands of trials, and the jasper still comes out wrong. Stain the white body with oxides until it matches the pale blue Wedgwood is after.
challenges.fact: Wedgwood spent years and thousands of experiments to develop Jasperware — a ceramic so consistent that every piece looked identical. He believed in what today we call quality control: testing every batch, recording every failure. His laboratory notebooks survive, filled with meticulous records of clay, glaze, and kiln temperature.

challenges.instruction: The medallions go out by the thousand, and Wedgwood's canal company now brings in limestone on rails from Caldon Low. Sort the wagons at Froghall onto the sidings and send them out to the boats in order.
challenges.fact: Charles Darwin was Josiah Wedgwood's grandson — his mother Susannah was Wedgwood's daughter, and his wife Emma was Wedgwood's granddaughter. Darwin married his own cousin from the Wedgwood family, a common practice in Victorian upper-class families.

challenges.instruction: Wedgwood sells to queens and shopkeepers alike. Trade his china as royal orders, rivals and canal news move the price, and finish richer than you started.
challenges.fact: Wedgwood was a major investor in the Grand Trunk Canal, which connected his Staffordshire potteries to the ports at Liverpool and Hull. He understood that transport was as important as manufacturing — cheap bulk movement of clay in and finished goods out made his mass-production model possible.

challenges.instruction: The system ends where the ware leaves Etruria: on the Trent and Mersey Canal. Work the boats up and down the narrow locks and waste as little of the scarce summit water as you can.
challenges.fact: Wedgwood brilliantly marketed at both ends of the market. He sold exclusive pieces to royalty and aristocracy — then used their endorsements to sell affordable versions to the growing middle class. His catalogue, free delivery, and money-back guarantee made quality ceramics accessible to ordinary households, pioneering the modern retail model.

challenges.instruction: Peterhof, before dawn: Alexei Orlov has ridden through the night with a note from the Guards. Read the grid code — it tells Catherine whether this is the morning she takes Russia.
challenges.fact: In July 1762, Catherine organized a coup against her husband Tsar Peter III — who was widely seen as weak and pro-Prussian. The Imperial Guard supported her; Peter was arrested and died days later (likely murdered). Catherine ruled Russia for 34 years as Catherine II.

Catherine ruled Russia for 34 years — longer than any other female ruler in Russian history. She expanded Russia's territory by 520,000 square kilometres and corresponded with Voltaire and Diderot while suppressing the very freedoms they championed.
challenges.instruction: Catherine writes to Voltaire of reform, but Russia lives on its harvest. Plan the village fields the way her Free Economic Society urges — rye, oats, clover and fallow — so there is grain to sell and fodder for the herd.

To wake Russia, Catherine backs the self-taught genius Ivan Kulibin. Build his single timber arch across the Neva, every strut pushing, so it can carry its load without a pier in the ice-choked river.
challenges.fact: In 1769 Catherine made Ivan Kulibin, a self-taught clockmaker from Nizhny Novgorod, head of the mechanical workshop of the Academy of Sciences. Besides his Neva bridge he built a searchlight with mirrors, a river boat that winched itself upstream, and mechanical legs for wounded soldiers.

challenges.instruction: Catherine's coup is underway. Promise what each Guard regiment and power in Petersburg wants — without driving the others away — before Peter III realises what is happening.
challenges.fact: On 28 June 1762 (9 July in the modern calendar) Catherine rode from Peterhof to the barracks of the Izmailovsky Guards, then the Semyonovsky and Preobrazhensky, and by mid-morning was proclaimed empress at the Kazan Cathedral in St Petersburg. Peter III, who had alienated the army by making peace with Prussia, signed his abdication the next day.

Catherine bought whole collections at once — Gotzkowsky's 225 paintings in 1764, Count Brühl's in 1769, Crozat's in 1772, Walpole's in 1779 — and wrote that it was not love of art but greed. Her Hermitage opened to the public in 1852 and today holds over three million objects.
challenges.instruction: Catherine retreats to her 'hermitage' beside the Winter Palace, where the pictures she buys by the hundred wait to be hung. Place each masterpiece in the room that shows it best.

challenges.fact: On 7 May 1770 the fourteen-year-old Archduchess Maria Antonia was handed over to France on an island in the Rhine near Strasbourg, where she left behind her Austrian clothes and attendants. She married the Dauphin, the future Louis XVI, at Versailles on 16 May.

challenges.instruction: The queen's parties set the fashion, and so does her music: she has brought her old teacher Gluck to Paris. Put the scenes of his Orphée in order for the Opéra.
challenges.fact: Gluck's French operas split Paris in the late 1770s into Gluckists and Piccinnists, partisans of the Italian composer Niccolò Piccinni, and the quarrel was fought out in pamphlets as fiercely as any political cause.

challenges.instruction: The royal family's escape plan: help Marie Antoinette navigate the Flight to Varennes.

challenges.instruction: While the queen waits in the Conciergerie, the Republic that will try her is building a faster France. Raise Chappe's semaphore towers so every city can signal every other with as few towers as possible.

challenges.fact: In 1622 Nzinga persuaded Governor João Correia de Sousa to treat Ndongo as an ally rather than a tributary vassal, and was baptised in Luanda as Dona Ana de Sousa. She used the faith as diplomacy: years later she returned to her own religion, then accepted Christianity again in the 1650s to make peace with Portugal.

challenges.instruction: Matamba's markets will pay for Nzinga's new kingdom and its army. Buy raffia cloth when the news drives it cheap and sell when war and shortage drive it dear.
challenges.fact: Driven out of Ndongo, Nzinga conquered the kingdom of Matamba around 1631 and made it her base, welcoming runaway slaves and allying with Imbangala war bands. Matamba grew rich on trade — above all, grimly, the sale of war captives to European slavers.

challenges.instruction: With the Dutch now holding Luanda, Nzinga must join her war camps to her new allies' posts. Link every camp across the rivers so the alliance can move as one army.
challenges.fact: After the Dutch seized Luanda in 1641, Nzinga allied with them against Portugal. In 1647 her army and Dutch troops routed the Portuguese at Kombi and besieged the fort of Massangano, until a Portuguese fleet from Brazil retook Luanda in 1648.

challenges.instruction: Nzinga knew the rivers of Ndongo better than any Portuguese captain. Run the war canoe down the Kwanza to the island stronghold, steering clear of rocks, hippos and crocodiles.
challenges.fact: Nzinga's forces moved by river and forest, striking Portuguese supply lines and vanishing before columns could react. The guerrilla war she waged kept the Portuguese out of her kingdom of Matamba for decades, until a 1656 treaty finally recognised her as its queen.

challenges.instruction: Lead Nzinga's forces in a flanking raid against a Portuguese supply column. Speed and terrain are your weapons — European cannon cannot aim at what it cannot see.
challenges.fact: Portuguese military reports describe Nzinga's forces as extraordinarily mobile and difficult to engage in pitched battle. She understood that her army could not match European firepower in open confrontation, so she avoided it — choosing ambushes, river crossings, and night raids that neutralized the Portuguese advantage.

params.title: The Siege of Massangano, 1647
params.intro: After routing the Portuguese at Kombi, Nzinga and her Dutch allies close on the river fort of Massangano, but the garrison has sown the approaches with buried powder charges. Open every safe square; each number counts the charges in the eight squares around it.
params.fact: In October 1647 Nzinga and her Dutch allies routed a Portuguese army at Kombi and laid siege to Massangano, the last Portuguese stronghold inland. The fort held out: in August 1648 Salvador Correia de Sá retook Luanda from the Dutch, and Nzinga had to withdraw to Matamba.

Borromini (1599–1667) invented a new architectural language: walls that curved inward and outward, spaces that expanded and contracted as you moved through them, and geometry derived from interlocking triangles rather than squares. His buildings feel alive — as if the stone itself is breathing.
challenges.instruction: Borromini's walls refuse to stand straight. Guess the five-letter word for what his façades do where Bernini's stand firm.

Every Borromini plan closes on itself, built from triangles and ovals with nothing left to chance. Ride the knight across every square and end one leap from where you began, a figure as closed as his geometry.
challenges.fact: Borromini's geometry was rooted in medieval sacred mathematics — he derived church plans from the proportions of the equilateral triangle, believing divine truth was encoded in geometric relationships. His buildings are not just beautiful; they are arguments about the nature of space and the presence of God within it.

params.title: The Hidden Skeleton
params.intro: Borromini drew his plans from interlocking triangles and ovals, every curve closing on itself. Visit every square once — and finish a knight’s move from where you began (the ringed square).
params.fact: Borromini built the plan of San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane (begun 1634) from two equilateral triangles sharing a base, with an oval traced inside them.

challenges.instruction: For the Oratorians Borromini is building the hall where Rome gathers to hear sacred stories sung. Put the sections of an oratorio of the day in the order the story unfolds.
challenges.fact: Borromini designed the Oratory of the Filippini beside the Chiesa Nuova from 1637 for the Congregation of the Oratory founded by St Philip Neri. Its concave brick façade hides the hall where the congregation's musical prayer meetings — the gatherings that gave the oratorio its name — were held.

challenges.instruction: Rome has become a board for two players: Bernini's fountain on one side of Piazza Navona, Borromini's Sant'Agnese on the other. Take the rivalry square by square and line up five before your rival does.
challenges.fact: On Piazza Navona Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers (1648–1651) stands before Borromini's Sant'Agnese in Agone (begun 1653). The tale that Bernini's River Plate raises a hand to shield himself from the falling church is a legend: the fountain was finished before Borromini began the façade. The rivalry itself was real — Borromini believed Bernini took credit for his ideas.

params.title: Piazza Navona
params.intro: A rivalry played out on one square: you are black and move first. Five or more in a row wins.
params.fact: Bernini’s Fountain of the Four Rivers (1651) and Borromini’s Sant’Agnese in Agone face each other across Piazza Navona, the ancient stadium of Domitian.

challenges.instruction: Borromini is dead, but his churches still curve across the city. Walk his Rome and cross every bridge exactly once.
challenges.fact: Borromini's last great work, Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza (1642–1660), rests on a star-hexagon plan of two interlocking triangles and is crowned by a spiralling lantern. He died in August 1667 after falling on his sword; his buildings outlived every critic.

Apollo and Daphne (1622–1625) shows the moment Daphne transforms into a laurel tree to escape Apollo — her fingers becoming branches, bark creeping up her legs. Bernini carved this in marble when he was in his mid-twenties. Viewers reported that the finished work looked impossible, as if he had found a way to capture a single instant of motion in stone.
challenges.instruction: Cardinal Scipione Borghese has filled his villa with the young Bernini's marbles. Place each work in the room that shows it best, with Apollo and Daphne where it can astonish.
Above St Peter's tomb the bronze baldachin rises, crawling with Urban VIII's Barberini bees, laurel and suns. Match the emblems as Bernini's foundry casts and gilds them.
challenges.fact: Bernini's baldachin (1624–1634) rises about 29 m over the tomb of St Peter on four twisted bronze columns modelled on the ancient columns of Old St Peter's. Urban VIII had bronze stripped from the Pantheon's portico, much of it for cannon at Castel Sant'Angelo, prompting Romans to quip: 'What the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did.'

challenges.instruction: Bernini wants St Teresa to glow as if lit from heaven, by a source no worshipper can see. Steer the daylight from his hidden window down onto the saint and the angel.
challenges.fact: The Cornaro Chapel in Santa Maria della Vittoria (1647–1652) was commissioned by Cardinal Federico Cornaro. A window concealed above the altar pours daylight down gilded bronze rays onto Teresa and the angel, while marble members of the Cornaro family watch from theatre boxes on the side walls.

challenges.instruction: Bernini's colonnade wraps St Peter's Square in four rows of columns. Leap through every bay of the square once, touching the numbered marks in order, as a pilgrim crossing the motherly arms of the Church.
challenges.fact: Bernini designed St. Peter's Square's twin colonnades to open at their ends, creating a welcoming gesture toward the city. He described them as 'the motherly arms of the Church' reaching out to embrace the faithful — Catholics to confirm their faith, heretics to reunite with the Church, and unbelievers to discover the light. The design is both engineering and theology.

params.title: The Colonnade of St Peter’s
params.intro: Bernini’s colonnade (1656–1667) frames St Peter’s Square. Leap through every bay of the square once, landing on the numbered marks in order — 1, then 2, then 3. A numbered mark cannot be entered early.
params.fact: Bernini built the colonnade of St Peter’s Square for Alexander VII between 1656 and 1667: 284 columns in four rows, topped by 140 statues of saints.

challenges.instruction: In his last winter a great comet hangs over Rome. Plot its path through the astronomers' sightings, the last wonder of the sky Bernini will see.
challenges.fact: Bernini died in Rome on 28 November 1680, aged 81, a fortnight after Gottfried Kirch first saw the Great Comet. He had served popes from Paul V to Innocent XI, and was buried in Santa Maria Maggiore beneath a plain slab in the floor.

challenges.instruction: In his late sixties Bernini turns the old bridge to Castel Sant'Angelo into a Way of the Cross lined with angels. Lead the pilgrims over every bridge once and home to St Peter's.
challenges.fact: In 1667 Clement IX commissioned ten angels for the Ponte Sant'Angelo, each holding an instrument of the Passion. Bernini designed them all and carved two himself — the angels with the Crown of Thorns and the Superscription — which the pope kept from the weather; they are now in Sant'Andrea delle Fratte.

Nian Xiyao (1671–1738) published Shixue ('The Science of Vision') in 1729, systematically explaining Western linear perspective — vanishing points, foreshortening, and the geometry of sight — to Chinese readers for the first time. He worked closely with the Jesuit painter Giuseppe Castiglione at the Yongzheng court, blending Eastern aesthetic sensibility with Western mathematical precision.
challenges.instruction: Perspective starts with straight lines on a grid, and Nian Xiyao tests his eye on a weiqi board left half-played. Line up five stones in a row before your opponent does.
Shixue rests on the same Western geometry the Jesuits use at the Beijing observatory. Set the planet's launch speed and angle so its ellipse passes through every recorded sighting.
challenges.fact: Traditional Chinese painting used 'axonometric' perspective — objects remained the same size regardless of distance, and there was no single vanishing point. This was a deliberate artistic choice, not a technical limitation: it allowed the eye to travel through a landscape rather than fix on one point. Nian Xiyao presented Western perspective as a complementary system, not a replacement.

challenges.instruction: Jingdezhen's kilns also make porcelain for Europe, painted with Western scenes and shipped from Canton. Stow the hold with the most valuable cargo until the manifest is met.
challenges.fact: Nian Xiyao's imperial kilns at Jingdezhen produced some of the most technically spectacular porcelain in Chinese history: new enamel colors mixed from European pigments, copper-red glazes that had been lost for centuries, and forms that reflected Western shapes while remaining distinctly Chinese. His career embodied the Yongzheng court's sophisticated engagement with global culture.

challenges.instruction: Nian Xiyao sends his designs from Beijing to Jingdezhen. Choose the metal oxide for each band of the imperial vase so every enamel fires true.
challenges.fact: Nian Xiyao ran the imperial kilns at Jingdezhen from 1726 while serving as a customs official, sending designs and orders from the court. His deputy Tang Ying, who arrived in 1728, succeeded him and later wrote illustrated accounts of each stage of porcelain making.

challenges.instruction: Between the kilns and the court, Nian Xiyao moves among Jesuit craftsmen whose pendulum clocks tick in the palace workshops. Move the bob until the new clock keeps time.
challenges.fact: Linear perspective was developed by Filippo Brunelleschi in Florence around 1420 and became the dominant visual system of European art. Nian Xiyao's Shixue explained that perspective was not merely an artistic convention but a mathematical truth — that sight itself operates geometrically. This was a revolutionary claim in a culture that viewed painting as an act of imagination rather than observation.

challenges.instruction: The art Nian Xiyao helped shape lives on at the Qianlong court, where the emperor keeps the Lantern Festival at the Yuanmingyuan. Light every lantern in the lattice.
challenges.fact: The 'famille rose' palette — pinks made with colloidal gold and an opaque lead-arsenate white, both learned from European enamelling — was perfected in the Yongzheng years, when Nian Xiyao ran the imperial kilns. Its soft, shaded colours became the signature of 18th-century Qing porcelain.

challenges.question: What term did Gandhi coin for his philosophy of nonviolent resistance?
challenges.fact: Gandhi coined 'Satyagraha' — from Sanskrit satya (truth) and agraha (holding firmly) — in South Africa in 1906. It means 'truth-force' or 'soul-force,' and distinguished his method from passive resistance: Satyagraha was an active, courageous confrontation with injustice using love rather than violence.

The Salt March of 1930 transformed Gandhi from a respected Indian leader into a global symbol. When he picked up a pinch of salt on the Dandi beach, he broke British law — and the world was watching. Within weeks, 60,000 Indians had been arrested for the same act of defiance.
challenges.instruction: A reporter on Dandi beach wires the news. Read the lamp.

challenges.fact: After Gandhi's arrest on 5 May 1930, the poet Sarojini Naidu led some 2,500 volunteers to the Dharasana Salt Works. Row after row walked forward to be beaten down by the police, and not one raised a hand to defend himself.
challenges.instruction: Gandhi is in jail, but the satyagrahis march on the Dharasana salt works and take the blows without striking back. Get Webb Miller's story past the police lines and out to the world.
Complete the crossword of Gandhi's India — the people, places and principles of a revolution without rifles.
challenges.fact: Gandhi's methods were studied and adopted by civil rights leaders around the world. Martin Luther King Jr. called Gandhi's philosophy 'the guiding light of our technique of nonviolent social change.' Nelson Mandela, Cesar Chavez, and Aung San Suu Kyi all cited Gandhi's example.

challenges.instruction: Long before Dandi, Gandhi organised in South Africa — even on the football pitch, where his teams played as the Passive Resisters. Score three from the spot.
challenges.fact: Gandhi lived in South Africa from 1893 to 1914. There he first organised mass nonviolent resistance against laws aimed at Indians, and worked out the methods he would bring home to India.

challenges.instruction: Cross two round-seeded hybrids and the wrinkled seeds come back. Breed the peas and find the proportion Mendel counted in the next generation.
challenges.fact: Mendel chose pea plants (Pisum sativum) with extraordinary care. They had clearly distinguishable traits — smooth or wrinkled seeds, yellow or green pods, tall or short stems — that produced consistent, countable offspring. Over eight years, he tracked 29,000 plants and applied mathematics to biology for the first time.

challenges.instruction: Mendel's 1865 lectures in Brno rested on counts no naturalist had bothered to make. Add up the tallies from his pea beds.
challenges.fact: When Mendel published his results in 1866, the scientific world largely ignored them. His paper was cited only a handful of times in the next 35 years. It was not until 1900 — 16 years after Mendel's death — that three botanists independently rediscovered his laws and finally found his original paper, launching the science of genetics.

challenges.instruction: Mendel wrote of hidden 'elements' passed from parent to offspring; the next century gave them a five-letter name. Guess it.
challenges.fact: The 3:1 ratio Mendel observed — three dominant to one recessive — was not a coincidence or approximation. It was a mathematical law. Mendel was the first scientist to apply statistical analysis to biology, and his insight that inheritance comes in discrete packets (what we now call genes) was centuries ahead of its time.

challenges.instruction: Breed peas the way Mendel did, crossing plants or letting one pollinate itself. Plan each cross on a Punnett square, the grid Reginald Punnett drew in 1905 to explain results like Mendel's, before you spend a season on it.
challenges.fact: A Punnett square maps out all possible genetic combinations from two parents. When Mendel crossed round-seeded (Rr) plants together, the square predicts 25% RR, 50% Rr and 25% rr offspring: 75% round, 25% wrinkled. The 3:1 ratio that baffled naturalists for centuries was hiding in plain arithmetic.

challenges.instruction: Classify each pea plant trait as dominant or recessive — just as Mendel did in his monastery garden, sorting thousands of seeds by hand.
challenges.fact: Mendel identified seven distinct traits in pea plants, each with a dominant and recessive form. Remarkably, the genes controlling these seven traits happen to lie on different chromosomes, which is why Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment holds perfectly for them — a stroke of extraordinary scientific luck.

challenges.instruction: Eight years of counting go into print at last. Set the title of Mendel's paper for the Brünn society's Proceedings and pull a clean proof.
challenges.fact: Mendel kept records of extraordinary precision across eight years of experiments. He tracked 29,000 plants through multiple generations, recording results in tables that would not be out of place in a modern biology lab. His data was so clean that statistician R.A. Fisher later controversially suggested it was too perfect.

challenges.fact: Robert Schumann heard the 20-year-old Brahms play in 1853 and immediately published an article declaring him 'the one called to give ideal expression to the times.' It was an extraordinary endorsement that launched Brahms' career — and also set impossible expectations that would haunt him for decades.

challenges.instruction: Before any symphony, Brahms made his name with a requiem written after his mother's death. Arrange the movements of A German Requiem in order.
challenges.fact: Brahms labored over his First Symphony for 21 years, from 1854 to 1876. He was paralyzed by the shadow of Beethoven — convinced that any symphony he wrote would be compared unfavorably to Beethoven's nine. When it finally premiered, the conductor Hans von Bülow called it 'Beethoven's Tenth' — the highest compliment and a backhanded burden.

challenges.instruction: Brahms hears tempo in the structure of the music, not in a ticking machine. Still, pick out every pendulum that truly beats with the reference — only its length sets the time.
challenges.fact: Brahms was his own harshest critic. By his own account he wrote some twenty string quartets before he let one be published — the pair of Op. 51, in 1873 — and he burned many drafts and early works he judged unworthy.

challenges.instruction: The song Brahms wrote for a friend's newborn became the world's lullaby. Play it through as the strings press the tempo.
challenges.fact: Brahms's Wiegenlied was first sung in public in Vienna in December 1869, with Clara Schumann at the piano. Few melodies have been sung over more cradles since.

challenges.instruction: Edison's agent has carried a phonograph to Vienna to catch the master at the piano. Gear the motor down so the wax cylinder turns true while Brahms plays his Hungarian Dance.
challenges.fact: On 2 December 1889 Brahms played part of his first Hungarian Dance into Edison's phonograph in Vienna. The worn cylinder, copied many times since, is the only recording of Brahms himself at the keyboard.

The Enigma machine had 17,576 possible rotor starting positions (26×26×26). But with plugboard settings, the actual number of configurations was 158 quintillion — the Bombe exploited cribs (known plaintext) to narrow the search.
challenges.instruction: Before the Bombe, Turing practises on a simple shift. The hidden word is the crib Bletchley Park hunted for every morning — turn the wheel until it reads.
Five letters name the machine Turing designed to search Enigma's settings. Guess it before the day's key changes at midnight.
challenges.fact: Turing's Bombe ran through Enigma rotor settings at speed, rejecting every one that contradicted the crib, until only a handful were left for the codebreakers to test by hand.

challenges.instruction: Every Enigma keypress closed an electrical path through the plugboard and rotors to a lamp. Complete the circuit so the signal gets through.
challenges.fact: Turing's Bombe was based on a Polish machine called the Bomba, which Turing and Gordon Welchman dramatically improved. At peak operation, 211 Bombe machines ran simultaneously at Bletchley Park.

challenges.instruction: Back to the idea of 1936: a machine that reads a tape and rewrites it by rule. Wire the gates so the circuit gives the right output on every row.
challenges.fact: In 1946 Turing designed the Automatic Computing Engine (ACE) for the National Physical Laboratory, one of the first complete designs for a stored-program computer; a Pilot ACE ran in 1950.

challenges.instruction: Put the steps in order so the machine accepts the right strings and rejects the rest — computation broken into rules simple enough for a machine to follow.
challenges.fact: Turing's 1936 paper introduced the concept of a universal machine: a theoretical device that could simulate any algorithm by reading and writing symbols on a tape.

challenges.instruction: Lorentz's answer to Michelson and Morley is pure calculation. Work the letter sum digit by digit, as carefully as he worked his equations.
challenges.fact: Hendrik Lorentz derived the 'Lorentz transformation' equations in 1895–1904, which showed that time, length, and mass change with velocity. Einstein took these equations and provided the physical interpretation: special relativity (1905).

challenges.instruction: Einstein builds on Lorentz's equations, and the whole of physics is talking. Match each physicist of the age with the discovery that made his name.
challenges.fact: Lorentz contraction predicts that a moving object appears shorter in the direction of motion. A cylinder moving at 87% of light speed would appear halved in length — its volume halved — to a stationary observer.

params.title: The Leiden Letters
params.intro: Physics around 1900 is a small world of letters, lectures and congresses. Match each physicist with the discovery that made his name.
params.twist: Shifting papers: whenever you turn up two slips that do not match, they trade places as they go face down. Remember where each one went.
params.fact: Lorentz chaired the first Solvay Conference in Brussels in 1911 and every one until his death in 1928; Einstein called him the greatest and noblest man of their time.

challenges.instruction: Late in life Lorentz turns his mathematics on the sea itself. Link the islands and shores of the Zuiderzee with dikes, as his committee's tide calculations allow.
challenges.fact: Lorentz shared the 1902 Nobel Prize in Physics with his former student Pieter Zeeman, whose discovery that a magnetic field splits spectral lines Lorentz had explained with his theory of the electron.

challenges.instruction: Lorentz's electron theory says a magnetic field bends a moving charge. Set the field strength to curve the particle onto the target.
challenges.fact: The Lorentz force (F = qv × B) causes charged particles to curve in a magnetic field — the foundation of cathode ray tubes, particle accelerators, and mass spectrometers.

challenges.instruction: Léon Foucault measured the speed of light by bouncing a beam off a spinning mirror. You have one mirror — route the beam through four fixed reflectors to reach the exit.
challenges.fact: Foucault measured the speed of light at 298,000 km/s in 1850 — within 0.6% of the true value — using a rotating mirror that shifted while light was in transit. Lorentz's equations later explained why light's speed is constant for all observers.

challenges.fact: Chanel's first success was hats: plain straw boaters stripped of the feathers and fruit then in fashion. When the actress Gabrielle Dorziat wore them on the Paris stage in 1912, the city followed.

challenges.instruction: Simplicity still has to be made by hand. Set up the workrooms so each jersey dress moves from cutting to finishing without a bottleneck.
challenges.fact: Each of Chanel's innovations stripped away constraint. Jersey replaced stiff silk; cardigan suits replaced corsets; black replaced colour as the dominant fashion statement. She built freedom into fashion at a time when clothing was still architecture built to restrict women's bodies.

challenges.instruction: The Jazz Age inspired Chanel's Paris salon. Arrange the notes of a 1920s jazz phrase.
challenges.fact: Chanel thrived in the Jazz Age Paris of the 1920s — a world of Picasso, Stravinsky, Diaghilev, and Hemingway. She dressed the dancers of the Ballets Russes and set the aesthetic for an entire era.

challenges.instruction: Chanel built an empire on her own terms and watched every franc of it. Make the house accounts add up.
challenges.fact: Victorian corsets could pull a waist to 45 cm (18 inches), causing fainting, rib deformities, and displaced organs. Chanel borrowed fabrics from men's sportswear — jersey, tweed — and designed for movement. 'I gave women a sense of freedom,' she said. 'I gave them back their bodies.' It was a cultural revolution sewn into cloth.

challenges.fact: Earhart flew a single-engine Lockheed Vega 5B, painted red with gold trim. The same aeroplane now hangs in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum in Washington.

params.title: Blind over the Atlantic, 1932
params.intro: Fly east from Newfoundland to Ireland. In cloud you cannot see the sea or the stars, and a heading set blind drifts one point off. Climbing out for a star fix holds your heading true, but ice forms on the wings: you have only a few.

challenges.instruction: Ice on the wings, a broken altimeter, flames at the exhaust. Ride the winds across the Atlantic and find land.
challenges.fact: In 1932, Earhart flew solo from Newfoundland to Northern Ireland in 14 hours 56 minutes — battling icing, storm turbulence, and a leaking fuel tank.

challenges.instruction: Earhart learned her trade in a yellow biplane called The Canary. Brace its wings so they hold, whatever the air throws at them.
challenges.fact: Earhart took her first flying lessons in January 1921 from Neta Snook, one of the first women aviators in California, and saved for months to buy a plane of her own.

challenges.instruction: She has landed in a pasture near Londonderry. Lay the cable that carries the news back to New York.
challenges.fact: Charles Lindbergh made the first solo transatlantic flight in 1927. Earhart was the first WOMAN to do so — in 1932, flying from Newfoundland to Northern Ireland in 14 hours 56 minutes. She also set the record for fastest transatlantic solo flight at that time.

challenges.instruction: 1937: Earhart sets out to circle the globe with Fred Noonan navigating. Take his star sights and fix the Electra's latitude, leg by leg.
challenges.fact: Earhart and Noonan vanished on 2 July 1937 near Howland Island in the central Pacific. The US Navy and Coast Guard mounted a vast search, but no trace of them was ever found.
