challenges.fact: Eisenstein believed that two images in sequence create a third meaning absent from either — as in the Kuleshov effect. A shot of a man's neutral face followed by soup suggests hunger; followed by a coffin suggests grief. Same face, different meanings.

params.title: The Proletkult Stage, 1923
params.intro: The stage lamps have three notches — dark, dim, bright. Each tap turns a lamp and its four neighbours up one notch, and bright wraps round to dark. Bring every lamp to bright.
params.fact: At Moscow's Proletkult Theatre in 1923 Eisenstein staged Ostrovsky's comedy Enough Stupidity in Every Wise Man as a 'montage of attractions' — circus turns, a tightrope walk and his first film, the short Glumov's Diary.

challenges.instruction: Eisenstein's Odessa Steps sequence builds to a critical cut. Choose how he resolved it.
challenges.fact: Eisenstein's montage theory holds that meaning is created between shots, not within them. The Battleship Potemkin (1925) remains the most studied example of this principle.

challenges.instruction: Montage means no shot repeats the idea beside it. Fill the grid so each row, column and box holds every number once — and let the meaning emerge between them.
challenges.fact: Eisenstein's montage theory holds that meaning is created between shots, not within them. The Kuleshov effect proves it: the same neutral face, cut to food, reads as hunger; cut to a coffin, reads as grief. The Odessa Steps sequence in Battleship Potemkin (1925) remains the most studied example of this principle.

Battleship Potemkin (1925) was banned in the UK until 1954, in Nazi Germany, and across much of Europe for portraying mutiny as heroic. In the UK, the censor wrote it presented 'Bolshevik propaganda' too powerfully. The bans made the film legendary — its Odessa Steps sequence is still cited as one of the greatest in film history.

challenges.fact: The Long March (1934–35) covered about 9,000 km — crossing 18 mountain ranges and 24 rivers. Of the 80,000 who began, fewer than 10,000 completed it. It transformed apparent defeat into the founding myth of Communist China.

params.title: The Blockhouse Lines, 1934
params.intro: Chiang Kai-shek's blockhouses ring the Jiangxi Soviet. Open every safe square; each number counts the strongpoints in the eight squares around it.
params.fact: In his fifth encirclement campaign of 1933–34 Chiang Kai-shek closed on the Jiangxi Soviet behind lines of fortified blockhouses. In October 1934 the Red Army broke out westward through four blockade lines, losing more than half its strength by the end of the year.

challenges.instruction: Orders for the breakout travel in code across the Red Army's columns. Decode the dispatch from the Jiangxi Soviet.
challenges.fact: The Long March was a 9,000 km strategic retreat that repositioned the Red Army — transforming apparent defeat into the foundation of eventual victory.

challenges.instruction: At the Dadu River the planks of the Luding Bridge have been stripped away. Hang a new deck from the iron chains so the army can cross.
challenges.fact: The most decisive battle of the Long March was the crossing of the Luding Bridge — a chain bridge over a gorge, its planks removed, defended by machine guns. Communist soldiers crawled across the chains under fire.

challenges.instruction: Edgar Snow has his interviews with Mao. Get the story of the Long March past the Nationalist lines and into print.
challenges.fact: When the Long March began in October 1934, approximately 86,000 soldiers set out. Fewer than 8,000 reached Yan'an in October 1935 — a loss of over 90%. Mao Zedong transformed this catastrophic retreat into a founding myth of Communist China, portraying it as proof of revolutionary will and endurance.

challenges.fact: On October 26, 1909, An Jung-geun shot Itō Hirobumi — Japan's first Prime Minister and the architect of Korean colonisation — at Harbin railway station. An was captured, tried, and executed in 1910, the same year Japan formally annexed Korea.

challenges.instruction: Ahn told his judges he was an officer of the Korean Righteous Army, not a murderer. Lead the resistance across the board and capture the enemy pieces.
challenges.fact: An Jung-geun saw himself not as an assassin but as a soldier of justice — his act of resistance at Harbin Station became a symbol of Korean defiance against colonization.

challenges.instruction: To answer Itō, Ahn had to understand his world. Fill in the words of Meiji Japan and the peninsula it claimed.
challenges.fact: An Jung-geun wrote a treatise on peace in East Asia while awaiting execution, calling for cooperation between China, Japan, and Korea against Western colonialism. He was a complex figure — a Catholic, a scholar, and a revolutionary.

Ahn Jung-geun was executed by Japan in 1910. In Korea he is a national hero; in China, a statue stands at Harbin station where the assassination occurred. In Japan he is officially considered a criminal. The same act reads entirely differently across national histories.

challenges.fact: Andrew Mellon served as Treasury Secretary under Harding, Coolidge, and Hoover (1921–1932) — the longest tenure since Alexander Hamilton. He oversaw the Roaring Twenties boom and the beginning of the Great Depression, for which he was blamed.

challenges.instruction: At the Treasury Mellon cuts taxes and still runs a surplus. Balance the books, letter by letter.
challenges.fact: Mellon donated his art collection and $15 million to build Washington's National Gallery of Art — one of the greatest acts of private cultural philanthropy in American history. His collection included Raphaels, Rembrandts, and van Eycks bought from the Hermitage.

challenges.instruction: Andrew Mellon's Revenue Act would cut the top income tax rate from 73% to 25%. Whip the Senate one vote at a time before the progressives peel them away.
challenges.fact: Mellon's Revenue Acts of 1921, 1924, and 1926 cut the top marginal rate from 73% to 25%. Tax revenues rose during the 1920s boom, but the same policies concentrated wealth so severely that the Depression proved catastrophic. Mellon advised Hoover to 'liquidate labour, liquidate stocks' in 1929 — advice that deepened the crisis.

challenges.instruction: Pittsburgh's fortunes rise and fall with steel. Trade Carnegie Steel shares through eight rounds of news and reach the target portfolio.
challenges.fact: Carnegie Steel's rise mirrored the Gilded Age: astonishing wealth creation alongside brutal labour conditions. The 1892 Homestead Strike left seven dead and fatally damaged Carnegie's public image, despite his later philanthropic legacy.

challenges.instruction: Wealth must eventually serve beauty. Bid at the estate sale and secure the starred pieces before the money runs out.
challenges.fact: The Gilded Age saw explosive growth in auction houses and financial markets as railroads, steel, and electricity transformed the American economy.

challenges.fact: The Meiji Constitution of 1889 was drafted under Itō's leadership after he studied European constitutional models — particularly Prussia's. It established Japan as a constitutional monarchy and remained in force until 1947.

challenges.instruction: As Minister of Public Works Itō brings Western engineering to Tokyo; in 1878 his ministry's college lights Japan's first electric lamp. Wire the circuit until it glows.
challenges.fact: Itō served as Japan's Prime Minister four separate times between 1885 and 1901. His assassination by An Jung-geun in 1909 made him a martyr in Japan and a symbol of imperialism in Korea — two truths that coexist uncomfortably.

challenges.instruction: Gaslight arrives with the Meiji reforms. Light every lamp along Yokohama's new street.
challenges.fact: Japan went from feudal isolation to modern nation-state between 1868 and 1912: abolishing samurai, building railroads, establishing universal education, and defeating both China and Russia in war. No country modernized so completely so quickly.

params.title: Bashamichi, Yokohama, 1872
params.intro: Each lamp you light shares its gas main with the lamps beside it, above and below: tapping one toggles it and its four neighbours. Light the whole street.
params.fact: Japan's first gas street lamps were lit in Yokohama in October 1872 by a company of the merchant Takashima Kaemon, with the French engineer Henri Pelegrin. Tokyo's new brick Ginza had gas lamps by 1874.

challenges.instruction: The modern army Itō's Japan built goes to war with Russia. Clear a path for the sappers before Port Arthur without setting off a blast.
challenges.fact: Japan transformed from a feudal samurai society to a modern industrial nation in a single generation — faster than any other country in history. By 1905, Japan had defeated Russia in war, astonishing the world and inspiring anti-colonial movements across Asia.

params.fact: At the siege of Port Arthur (1904–05) Japanese engineers dug saps and tunnels beneath the Russian forts and blew them up with mines. The fortress surrendered on 2 January 1905 after five months.

challenges.fact: My Fair Lady (1956) ran for 2,717 performances on Broadway. Shaw famously wrote his own stage directions to prevent producers from adding a romantic happy ending.

challenges.instruction: Higgins can place a speaker within six miles by a single sound. Guess the five-letter word for what he means to change in Eliza.
challenges.fact: Shaw wrote 'Back to Methuselah' (1921), a five-play cycle running from Adam and Eve to the year 31,920. He was the first person to win both a Nobel Prize (1925) and an Academy Award (1938, for the screenplay of Pygmalion).

challenges.instruction: A Hungarian phonetics expert approaches Eliza Doolittle at the ambassador's party. What does he conclude?
challenges.fact: Shaw's irony: Eliza succeeds so perfectly that the expert concludes she must be foreign nobility — her English is too refined for a native. Class is performance, not origin.

Shaw explicitly wrote that Eliza marries Freddy Eynsford-Hill, not Higgins. He was furious when stage productions implied a romance. His epilogue spells out that Higgins is too self-absorbed for love. The musical My Fair Lady contradicts Shaw's own ending.

challenges.question: In what year did Mother Teresa found the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta?
challenges.fact: Mother Teresa founded the Missionaries of Charity on 7 October 1950. Beginning with just 13 members in Calcutta, the congregation grew to over 4,500 sisters operating in 133 countries by the time of her death in 1997.

challenges.instruction: With no building and no money, Teresa gathers the children of Motijhil in the open and teaches them in the dirt. Work out each sum and share out the bananas — a lesson and a meal together.
challenges.fact: When Mother Teresa left Loreto in 1948, she first took a short course in nursing with the Medical Mission Sisters in Patna, then came back to Calcutta to teach the children of Motijhil and visit the sick in their homes.

challenges.instruction: Nirmal Hriday is open, and the dying are brought in from the streets day and night. Draw up the sisters' rota so every duty is covered and no one is left alone.
challenges.fact: Each step built on the last: leaving the convent (1948) gave her freedom to serve; the Missionaries (1950) gave her sisters; Nirmal Hriday (1952) gave the dying dignity; and the Nobel Prize (1979) gave her voice to the world.

challenges.instruction: News of the Nobel Prize reaches Calcutta by telex. Read the lamps to learn in whose name Teresa accepts it.
challenges.fact: By her death in 1997 the Missionaries of Charity had grown from a handful of sisters in Calcutta to more than 4,000, running some 610 missions in 123 countries — hospices, orphanages, and homes for people with leprosy and HIV/AIDS.

challenges.instruction: Tenzing's seventh attempt begins with a long march. Lead the porters from Kathmandu to Thyangboche to acclimatise, then up through the Icefall to the South Col and the top.
challenges.fact: Hillary and Tenzing summited at 11:30 AM on 29 May 1953, spending only 15 minutes on top before descending — long enough for photographs and to bury a small cross and some sweets as offerings. The news reached London in time to appear on the morning of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation.

challenges.instruction: Roped together for weeks, Hillary and Tenzing depend on the lines fixed below them. Link the high camps with exactly the ropes each one needs.
challenges.fact: Hillary always insisted that he and Tenzing summited together as a team, refusing to say who stepped onto the peak first. He later wrote: 'We didn't talk about it much — it didn't seem important.' For the rest of his life, Hillary devoted enormous energy to building schools, hospitals, and water pipelines for the Sherpa communities of Nepal.

challenges.instruction: First light, 29 May. Pick a way along the knife-edge ridge and up the Hillary Step to the summit — every step at this height costs twice the breath.
challenges.fact: The 1953 expedition was a meticulous logistical operation: 400 porters, 362 loads of equipment, months of acclimatization. John Hunt's planning was military in precision. But in the end, it came down to two men in the predawn cold, kicking steps into ice above the Hillary Step.

challenges.instruction: A runner is already on his way down to Namche with The Times's coded message. Decode it — the news must reach London before anyone else hears.
challenges.fact: James Morris of The Times sent the news in a pre-arranged code: 'Snow conditions bad. Advanced base abandoned yesterday. Awaiting improvement' meant that Hillary and Tenzing had reached the top. It reached London on the eve of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation, and the paper broke the story on coronation morning, 2 June 1953.

challenges.instruction: Long before anyone stood on top, surveyors measured the mountain from the plains of India. Chain the triangles from the baseline up to Peak XV.
challenges.fact: The Survey of India first computed the height of Peak XV in 1856 from stations more than 160 km away and named it after Sir George Everest, its former Surveyor General. Tibetans call it Chomolungma, 'Goddess Mother of the World', and Nepalis Sagarmatha, 'Forehead of the Sky'. Its height, 8,848.86 m, was last fixed jointly by Nepal and China in 2020.

challenges.instruction: As UNICEF's Goodwill Ambassador, Audrey goes where the cameras rarely go. Plan her missions from home in Switzerland to Ethiopia, then Bangladesh, and at last to Somalia.
challenges.fact: Hepburn became a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador in 1988 for a token salary of one dollar a year. As a starving child in Holland in 1945 she had been fed by the Allied relief agencies that were the forerunners of UNICEF.

challenges.instruction: Dawn on Fifth Avenue, a black dress and a pastry at Tiffany's window — the scene that made Audrey an icon. Fit the pieces together until the opening of Breakfast at Tiffany's is whole.
challenges.fact: 'Moon River' won the 1962 Academy Award for Best Original Song. When a Paramount executive suggested cutting it, Hepburn reportedly said: 'Over my dead body!' Henry Mancini wrote the melody to suit her small vocal range.

challenges.instruction: Arnhem, 1944 — long before Hollywood. Help teenage Audrey slip through the occupied streets for the resistance, past the patrols and the mines, and home again.
challenges.fact: Hepburn spent the war in the Netherlands. In 1942 the occupiers executed her uncle, and her half-brother was sent to a labour camp in Germany. In the Hunger Winter of 1944–45 she lived on scraps, including flour made from tulip bulbs.

challenges.instruction: In Funny Face Audrey sweeps down the Louvre's grand staircase beneath the Winged Victory. Hang the masterpieces in the wings where they shine brightest and open the doors.
challenges.fact: In Funny Face (1957) Hepburn runs down the Daru staircase of the Louvre past the Winged Victory of Samothrace, a red chiffon scarf streaming behind her, while Fred Astaire's photographer shouts 'Take the picture!'

challenges.instruction: Years after Audrey's death, her black Givenchy gown goes under the hammer to build schools for poor children in India. Win the starred lots for the cause.
challenges.fact: In December 2006 the black Givenchy gown from Breakfast at Tiffany's sold at Christie's in London for £467,200, several times its estimate. The money went to City of Joy Aid, Dominique Lapierre's charity, to build schools for children in India.

challenges.instruction: Ten-year-old Michael has watched James Brown's feet until his own can do the same — and then something more. Hit every step on the beat.
challenges.fact: The Jackson 5 auditioned for Motown in Detroit in July 1968 and were signed by Berry Gordy. In 1969 Diana Ross helped introduce them to the public, and their debut album was called Diana Ross Presents The Jackson 5.

challenges.instruction: In the Billie Jean video every paving stone lights up as Michael steps on it. Throw the switches so exactly the marked stones glow.
challenges.fact: In the 1983 video for 'Billie Jean' the pavement lights up under Michael's feet. It became one of the first videos by a Black artist in heavy rotation on MTV, and that May, on the Motown 25 television special, he danced the moonwalk to the same song.

challenges.instruction: By the Bad tour, Michael's chimpanzee Bubbles travels the world with him. Work out each sum and give Bubbles the right number of bananas.
challenges.fact: The Bad World Tour of 1987–89, Jackson's first as a solo artist, played 123 concerts to about 4.4 million people across four continents.

challenges.instruction: Craven Cottage, 1999: Michael is the guest of Fulham's owner, and the crowd can hardly believe it. Step up and take the penalties for the home side.
challenges.fact: Jackson came to Fulham through his friendship with the club's owner, Mohamed Al-Fayed. When the statue Al-Fayed had raised to him at Craven Cottage was taken down in 2013, it went to the National Football Museum in Manchester.

challenges.instruction: In Villa Fiorito the boys kick balls of rags — until Diego's cousin gives him a real leather football. Work out the size of the ball he will not let go of.
challenges.fact: For his third birthday Diego's cousin Beto gave him a leather football, and he slept hugging it. By the age of eight he was playing for Los Cebollitas, a youth side that went 136 games unbeaten.

challenges.instruction: Mexico City, 22 June 1986: Argentina against England, four years after the Falklands. Beat the English goalkeeper and put Argentina through.
challenges.fact: Argentina beat England 2–1 in the quarter-final at the Estadio Azteca, then Belgium in the semi-final and West Germany in the final. Maradona, the captain, was named player of the tournament.

challenges.instruction: Diego takes the ball in his own half and runs. Slide him through the English defence — Reid, Butcher, Fenwick, then Shilton in goal — and into the net.
challenges.fact: On Argentine radio, the commentator Víctor Hugo Morales wept as he called the run, crying 'Barrilete cósmico — from what planet did you come?' The phrase 'cosmic kite' stuck to Maradona for life.

challenges.instruction: The journalist wants to know how he explains the first goal. Decode Diego's answer from the reporter's notebook.
challenges.fact: For nearly twenty years Maradona was coy about the handball. In 2005 he admitted on Argentine television that he had punched the ball in on purpose.

challenges.instruction: Six minutes from the end of the final, Burruchaga scores from Diego's pass. In the stands a furled banner is waiting — wind it on the right pole and read what Argentina is about to become.
challenges.fact: Argentina coach César Luis Menotti left Maradona out of the 1978 squad, saying he was too young to carry the pressure. Argentina won the tournament on home soil. Maradona said the exclusion 'broke my heart' — and that winning the 1986 World Cup finally healed the wound. In 1978, a 17-year-old sat out history; in 1986, a 25-year-old made it.

challenges.instruction: For months every chimpanzee has fled when Jane comes near. Read the signs in the Gombe forest — nests, dropped fruit — and find each group without scaring it off.
challenges.fact: Jane Goodall arrived at Gombe with no scientific degree — just a passion for animals and a naturalist's notebook. Her 60+ years of continuous research at Gombe is the longest running wildlife study in history, revealing that chimpanzees have personalities, cultures, and emotions.

challenges.instruction: Jane has cabled Louis Leakey about David Greybeard and his twig. Read Leakey's reply as it comes down the line.
challenges.fact: In 1960, Goodall observed chimpanzees stripping leaves from twigs to fish termites from mounds — the first recorded instance of animals making and using tools. When she reported this to Louis Leakey, he replied: 'Now we must redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as humans.'

challenges.instruction: David Greybeard now walks into camp for bananas, and the others follow his lead. Work out each sum and give David the right number.
challenges.fact: Jane Goodall's research at Gombe revealed that chimpanzee communities have distinct cultures — different groups use different tools, have different social customs, and even different vocalizations. Culture, once thought uniquely human, turns out to be a primate invention at least 7 million years old.

challenges.instruction: On the lecture circuit Jane makes the case that chimpanzees are our close kin, down to their blood groups and whether they can taste the bitter chemical PTC. Follow those genes from parents to young through a zoo colony.
challenges.fact: In 1986 Goodall helped organise the 'Understanding Chimpanzees' conference in Chicago. Reports there of vanishing forests and of chimpanzees hunted for meat and sold as pets turned her from field scientist into campaigner; since then she has travelled some 300 days a year.

challenges.instruction: The hills around Gombe have been cleared for farms and firewood. Slide the patches of forest back together so the chimpanzees' range is whole again.
challenges.fact: By the 1990s Gombe was an island of forest among bare hills. In 1994 the Jane Goodall Institute began TACARE, working with the surrounding villages on tree planting, farming and health, so that the people living beside the chimpanzees lead their protection.

challenges.instruction: Sixty years of Gombe notebooks now live inside a computer. Read Jane's message to the next generation, lamp by lamp.
challenges.fact: Goodall gave the Gombe chimpanzees names instead of numbers, which shocked the scientists of the day. Her study, begun in 1960, is now the longest-running field study of any wild animal, and her Roots & Shoots programme runs in more than 60 countries.

challenges.instruction: Perfecting the simple is the hardest thing in cooking. Make Robuchon's mashed potatoes the Jamin way, every step in its place.
challenges.fact: At his peak, Joël Robuchon held 32 Michelin stars across his restaurants worldwide — more than any chef in history. His empire spanned Paris, Monte Carlo, Las Vegas, Tokyo, Hong Kong, and beyond, each kitchen reflecting his obsessive pursuit of perfection.

challenges.instruction: Robuchon answers the critic with a counter, not a speech. Take L'Atelier from Saint-Germain round the world and finish the season ahead of the rival houses.
challenges.fact: Robuchon's retirement in 1996 was unprecedented in fine dining. He said he was exhausted and wanted to explore life beyond the kitchen. Seven years later, his return with the L'Atelier concept — casual counter seating around an open kitchen — reinvented fine dining for a new generation.

challenges.instruction: L'Atelier puts the cooks behind a counter, in full view of the guests. Share the work along the counter so no station holds up the meal.
challenges.fact: Robuchon spent years studying Japanese culinary philosophy — the concept of shokunin kishitsu (craftsman's spirit) deeply influenced his cooking. His L'Atelier restaurants, modelled on Japanese counter dining, blended French technique with Japanese minimalism and obsessive attention to the guest experience.

challenges.instruction: However many kitchens he runs, Robuchon still chooses his produce himself. Before dawn at Rungis, the great wholesale market of Paris, buy what the kitchen needs as prices fall, but before the other chefs clear the stalls.
challenges.fact: When Robuchon died in 2018, his restaurants around the world held 31 Michelin stars between them — more than any other chef.

params.title: Rungis Before Dawn
params.intro: Buy the day’s produce at Rungis. Every hour, prices fall. But when a crowd of chefs gathers at a stall it is about to sell out. Wait for bargains, but buy before the crowd does, or before the market closes.
params.waitMsg: Another hour passes at Rungis. Prices fall.

challenges.instruction: Every plate is a letter, and every one must say something true. Line up the ingredients at the pass until each plate is perfect.
challenges.fact: This is one of the most misunderstood facts about the Michelin system. Stars belong to the restaurant address and experience, not the individual chef. When Robuchon retired and closed his restaurants, their stars vanished. When he returned with L'Atelier, he earned new stars from scratch — accumulating more than any chef in history.

challenges.instruction: The other networks' lines have gone dead. Close every relay on CNN's four-wire and keep the voices from the ninth floor on the air.
challenges.fact: Peter Arnett broadcast live from Baghdad for CNN during the Gulf War air campaign on January 17, 1991 — the first time a war had been broadcast live on television. His reports from inside the enemy capital were watched by hundreds of millions worldwide.

challenges.instruction: Arnett learned to stay put in Vietnam, filing for the AP while others left. Read one of his Saigon dispatches off the teleprinter, lamp by lamp.
challenges.fact: War journalism transformed how governments prosecute and justify wars. Russell's dispatches triggered military reforms; Adams' photo changed American public opinion on Vietnam; Arnett's Gulf War broadcasts created the first live war on television — watched simultaneously by world leaders and ordinary viewers.

challenges.instruction: 'Someone has to be here. I will stay.' Get through the blacked-out city and back to the Al-Rashid with the story.
challenges.fact: Arnett's reports were read by Iraqi censors before broadcast, and CNN told viewers so. His report from a bombed factory that Iraq called a baby-milk plant — the US said it made biological weapons — drew fierce criticism in Washington.

challenges.instruction: Months before the bombing, CNN has paid for its own 'four-wire', a telephone circuit out of Baghdad that needs no operator to patch it through. Lay it west to Amman through every exchange on the desert road, one unbroken line.
challenges.fact: Live television journalism from a war zone required split-second decisions: what to broadcast, how to frame it, what to leave out. Arnett's reporting from Baghdad was criticised by the US military as too sympathetic to Iraq and praised by journalists as the only independent witness in the city. Both sides were watching the same broadcast.

params.title: The Four-Wire, 1991
params.intro: Run one single line from Baghdad to Amman through every exchange (no branches), using the least wire. When the bombs cut every other line, this one must still carry the broadcast out.

challenges.instruction: If you are in the right place with a microphone, the world cannot look away. Put Arnett's routine in order so the story gets out — and viewers know what it is.
challenges.fact: In March 1997 Arnett, then with CNN, interviewed Osama bin Laden at a hideout in eastern Afghanistan — bin Laden's first television interview — in which he declared holy war on the United States. Four and a half years later came the attacks of 11 September 2001.

challenges.instruction: A hundred products, and nobody loves any of them. Sort Apple's line into Jobs's four boxes — consumer or pro — and cut everything else.
challenges.fact: When Jobs returned to Apple in 1997, the company had 350 products. He cut it to 10 — a 2×2 grid of consumer and professional, desktop and portable. 'Deciding what not to do is as important as deciding what to do,' he said. The focus that followed produced the iMac, iPod, iPhone, and iPad within a decade.

challenges.instruction: Jony Ive's translucent shell lets you see right inside, down to the picture tube. Bend the electron beam with the magnets so it lands on target.
challenges.fact: The iMac went on sale in August 1998 in Bondi Blue, named after the sea at Sydney's Bondi Beach, and became the fastest-selling computer in Apple's history; five fruit colours followed in January 1999.

challenges.instruction: Under the blue teardrop it still has to work perfectly. Wire the gates so the circuit agrees with the table on every row.
challenges.fact: Jobs insisted that the inside of a machine be as well made as the outside — a lesson, he said, from his father, who finished the backs of cabinets that no one would ever see.

challenges.instruction: Technology and art are not separate things — the Mac proved it with letters made of dots. Read the lamps to spell out the campaign that brought Apple back.
challenges.fact: Jobs dropped out of Reed College in 1972 but kept auditing classes — including a calligraphy course by Lloyd Reynolds. That course taught him about serif and sans-serif typefaces, proportional spacing, and typographic beauty. Ten years later, the Macintosh became the first computer with multiple typefaces. 'If I had never dropped in on that course, every Mac would have had the same boring font.'

challenges.instruction: In his years away from Apple, Jobs bet on a small graphics company called Pixar. Balance the Toy Story pipeline so no team holds up the film.
challenges.fact: Jobs' exile produced two revolutions. NeXT's operating system became the foundation of macOS when Apple acquired NeXT in 1997 — bringing Jobs back. Pixar, bought from George Lucas for $10 million in 1986, produced Toy Story (1995), the first fully computer-animated feature film. Disney acquired Pixar for $7.4 billion in 2006, making Jobs Disney's largest individual shareholder.

challenges.instruction: 'Everybody should learn to program a computer, because it teaches you how to think.' Put each program's lines in the right order.
challenges.fact: Steve Jobs said: 'Everybody in this country should learn how to program a computer... because it teaches you how to think.'

challenges.instruction: Today the machines Jobs built change hands for fortunes. Outbid the collectors for the starred relics.
challenges.fact: In 2014 a working Apple-1 — one of about 200 that Jobs and Steve Wozniak built in 1976 — sold at auction in New York for $905,000. Jobs's handwritten 1973 job application has also sold for six figures.

challenges.fact: Harper Lee based Atticus partly on her own father, a lawyer who defended two Black men in Alabama. Peck and Harper Lee became lifelong friends after the 1962 film.

challenges.instruction: To play Atticus, Peck has to think like him. Put the defence's questions in the order that shows the jury who really struck Mayella Ewell.
challenges.fact: The AFI voted Atticus Finch the greatest movie hero of the 20th century. Peck later said the role was the one closest to his own moral convictions — he fought for civil rights throughout his career.

challenges.instruction: Atticus Finch makes his closing argument. Win enough jurors to acquit Tom Robinson.
challenges.fact: Harper Lee's novel (1960) is based partly on the 1931 Scottsboro Boys case. Despite Atticus's brilliant argument, the jury convicts — Lee's point being that moral courage alone cannot overcome structural injustice.

challenges.instruction: The picture is ready for the cinemas. Set the window card for the lobby — Gregory Peck as Atticus Finch — and pull a clean proof.
challenges.fact: To Kill a Mockingbird (1960) won the Pulitzer Prize in 1961 and became an immediate bestseller. It has sold more than 40 million copies and remains widely taught in schools. Harper Lee published almost nothing for 55 years afterward, until Go Set a Watchman appeared in 2015, shortly before her death in 2016.
